knowledge_statements.title: Product-Node Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction of bilinear nodes from a factorable expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a directed acyclic expression graph for a factorable expression and a product node with children representing functions \(u(x)\) and \(v(x)\), introduce an auxiliary variable \(y_p\), replace every outgoing use of that node by \(y_p\), and impose \(y_p=u(x)v(x)\). Process nodes in topological order and output the resulting lifted system. The projection of its equality-feasible set onto the original variables and root value is exactly the graph of the original expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each selected product node by one auxiliary variable and its defining product equality; projecting the lifted graph recovers the original expression exactly.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
Every selected node represents a well-defined binary product on the stated domain.

notation.meaning: auxiliary value assigned to product node p

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Factorable Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive lifting into unary and binary elementary operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a factorable expression \(f\), traverse its expression graph from leaves to root. Retain original variables at leaf nodes. For each nonleaf node \(i\) with elementary operation \(\phi_i\) and already represented children \(c(i)\), introduce \(y_i\) and impose \(y_i=\phi_i((y_j)_{j\in c(i)})\), interpreting original-variable children directly. The root variable is the output. The simultaneous defining equalities determine every auxiliary value uniquely for each domain-feasible \(x\), and their projection gives the graph of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively assign an auxiliary to every elementary operation. The defining equalities uniquely evaluate the graph and project exactly to the original function graph.
assumptions_latex: f is represented by a finite acyclic factorable expression graph.
Each elementary operation is single-valued on its prescribed domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output size and construction time of recursive elemental decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite acyclic expression graph have q nonleaf operation nodes and e arcs. Recursive factorable decomposition introduces exactly one auxiliary variable and one defining elemental relation per nonleaf node, hence q auxiliaries and q relations. A topological traversal constructs the decomposition in O(q+e) graph operations when each elemental relation has constant-size encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive decomposition uses one auxiliary and one defining relation per operation node and is constructible in time linear in the expression graph.
assumptions_latex: \text{The expression graph is finite and acyclic}.
\text{Each elemental relation has constant-size encoding}.
knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Graph Decomposition Size
Common-Subexpression Sharing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sharing of repeated nodes in an expression DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose several occurrences in a factorable formulation represent the same single-valued subexpression \(g(x)\) on a common domain. Introduce one auxiliary variable \(z\), impose the single defining relation \(z=g(x)\), and replace every occurrence by \(z\). Compared with duplicating the auxiliary and its identical defining relation, sharing preserves the projected equality-feasible set while using one auxiliary and one defining relation for that equivalence class of occurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical subexpressions may share one auxiliary and defining constraint without changing the exact projection, reducing duplicated variables and constraints.
assumptions_latex: All shared occurrences denote the same function g on the same domain.
The comparison concerns exact defining relations before relaxation.

notation.meaning: shared auxiliary value of the common subexpression
lifted system using one shared node

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Weakness from Duplicated Relaxed Copies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness that independent copies of one relaxed subexpression can admit a spurious projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=\{0\}, let the exact repeated subexpression have value g(0)=1/2, and relax its graph to R=\{(0,z):0\leq z\leq1\}. With two copies, impose downstream conditions z_1=0 and z_2=1. The duplicated relaxed system projects to \{0\}, whereas sharing one z would require z=0 and z=1 simultaneously and therefore has empty projection. Thus P_{\mathrm{share}}\subsetneq P_{\mathrm{dup}}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two independent relaxed copies can take inconsistent values that a single shared node forbids, so sharing can strictly strengthen the projection.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ imposes }z_1=0\text{ and }z_2=1.

notation.meaning: outer relation used for each relaxed copy

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Weakness from Duplicated Relaxed Copies

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shared Nodes Dominate Duplicated Relaxed Nodes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-strength effect of identifying repeated auxiliaries after relaxing their defining equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose k occurrences of one subexpression use the same local outer relation R(x,z_j), and let H(x,z_1,\ldots,z_k,w) be the downstream system. Let P_{\mathrm{dup}} be the x-projection obtained with independent z_j, and let P_{\mathrm{share}} be the x-projection obtained by consistently replacing every z_j by one z and imposing R(x,z) once. Then P_{\mathrm{share}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{dup}}. If R=\{(x,g(x)):x\in D\} is an exact single-valued graph relation, equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identifying repeated relaxed nodes cannot weaken the projected formulation and can strengthen it; exact single-valued node equations make sharing and duplication equivalent.
assumptions_latex: R(x,z_j)\text{ is identical for every duplicated occurrence}.
\text{Every downstream occurrence is replaced consistently when the node is shared}.

notation.meaning: projection with independent copies of the repeated node
projection with one shared node variable

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Nodes Dominate Duplicated Relaxed Nodes
Termwise Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One auxiliary value for each term of a finite sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{t=1}^m f_t(x)\) on a common domain \(D\). The termwise lifting introduces \(y_t\) with \(y_t=f_t(x)\) for every \(t\), and represents the epigraph of \(f\) by \(y_t=f_t(x)\) together with \(\eta\geq\sum_{t=1}^m y_t\). Consequently, projecting the lifted set onto \((x,\eta)\) yields exactly \(\{(x,\eta):x\in D,\ \eta\geq f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift each summand separately and aggregate its auxiliary value; projection gives exactly the original epigraph.
assumptions_latex: m is finite.
Each f_t is well-defined on D.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and outer epigraph aggregation for a finite sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x)=\sum_{t=1}^m f_t(x) on D, and let E_t\subseteq D\times\mathbb R satisfy \operatorname{epi}_D f_t\subseteq E_t. Then L=\{(x,\eta,y):x\in D,\ (x,y_t)\in E_t\ (t=1,\ldots,m),\ \eta\geq\sum_{t=1}^m y_t\} satisfies \operatorname{epi}_D f\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_{x,\eta}L. If E_t=\operatorname{epi}_D f_t for every t, then \operatorname{proj}_{x,\eta}L=\operatorname{epi}_D f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separately lifted outer epigraphs give an outer epigraph of the sum; exact term epigraphs give the exact summed epigraph.
assumptions_latex: m<\infty.
f_t(x)\in\mathbb R\text{ for every }x\in D\text{ and }t.

notation.meaning: exact or outer epigraph set for term t

knowledge_statements.title: Termwise Epigraph Lifting
Shared-Factor Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single lifted value represents a factor common to several products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{t=1}^m g(x)h_t(x)\) on \(D\). Introduce one shared-factor variable \(z=g(x)\) and product variables \(y_t=z h_t(x)\). Then the epigraph is represented by \(z=g(x)\), \(y_t=z h_t(x)\) for all \(t\), and \(\eta\geq\sum_{t=1}^m y_t\). Its projection onto \((x,\eta)\) is exactly the epigraph of \(f\); duplicating \(g(x)\) termwise is unnecessary in the exact lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate a common factor once, reuse its auxiliary in every product, and project to recover the original epigraph exactly.
assumptions_latex: g and every h_t are single-valued on D.
m is finite.

notation.meaning: auxiliary value of the t-th product

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit separation between unlinked and shared relaxations of a repeated factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[-1,1]\), \(g(x)=x^2\), and use the convex-hull relaxation \(x^2\le z_t\le1\) for two copies. For the expression \(g(x)-g(x)\), the unlinked epigraph relaxation is \(\eta\ge z_1-z_2\); at \(x=0\), \((z_1,z_2,\eta)=(0,1,-1)\) is feasible. The shared formulation imposes \(z_1=z_2=z\) and hence \(\eta\ge0\), so \((x,eta)=(0,-1)\) is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two relaxed copies of x² can take inconsistent values and create a false negative epigraph value; sharing the factor removes that point.
assumptions_latex: Each copied square graph is relaxed by \(x^2\le z_t\le1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Strengthening by Shared-Factor Consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Strength Gain Under Exact Factor Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact representational economy and relaxation strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every copied relation \(z_t=g(x)\) is imposed exactly, replacing the copies by one shared variable \(z=g(x)\) changes only the extended representation and auxiliary count. The projected exact feasible set is unchanged. Strengthening from sharing can arise only when copied factor relations are relaxed or incompletely linked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sharing an exactly represented factor saves duplicate variables but does not change the projected exact set; possible strengthening is a relaxation-level effect.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is single-valued on the domain.
Every copied relation \(z_t=g(x)\) is exact.
knowledge_statements.title: No Strength Gain Under Exact Factor Graphs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consistency Strength from a Shared Factor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation-strength effect of identifying copied values of a common factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a termwise relaxation introduces copies \(z_t\) of the same single-valued factor \(g(x)\), with otherwise identical local factor relaxations. Imposing \(z_t=z\) for all \(t\) intersects the termwise lifted set with consistency equations. Therefore
\[\operatorname{proj}(R_{\mathrm{shared}})\subseteq\operatorname{proj}(R_{\mathrm{termwise}}),\]
and containment can be strict when the unlinked blocks admit incompatible relaxed values of \(g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identifying relaxed copies of a common factor cannot weaken the relaxation and can exclude inconsistent copied values.
assumptions_latex: Every termwise block represents the same single-valued factor \(g(x)\).
The compared local factor relaxations are otherwise identical.

notation.meaning: termwise copy of the common factor value

knowledge_statements.title: Consistency Strength from a Shared Factor
Block-Separable Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended formulation separated by variable blocks and linked through shared variables or constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variables be partitioned as \(x=(x_{B_1},\ldots,x_{B_q})\), and let \(f(x)=\sum_{b=1}^q f_b(x_{B_b})\) on \(D\). Introduce \(y_b=f_b(x_{B_b})\) independently for each block and impose \(\eta\geq\sum_{b=1}^q y_b\), retaining any original coupling constraints defining \(D\). Projection onto \((x,\eta)\) gives exactly the original epigraph, while each nonlinear defining relation involves only its block variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift each block-local function independently, retain the original coupling constraints, and aggregate block values to obtain an exact epigraph representation.
assumptions_latex: The blocks B_b form a partition of the variable indices.
Each f_b depends only on x_{B_b}.

notation.meaning: lifted value of block function b

knowledge_statements.title: Original-Space Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation using no variables beyond those of the modeled set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), an original-space representation is a finite system of equalities and inequalities \(R(x)\) involving only \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:R(x)\}\). For an optimization model with a distinguished original-variable domain \(X\), the represented feasible set is \(S=\{x\in X:R(x)\}\); variables introduced solely as abbreviations are not permitted unless eliminated from the displayed system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original-space representation describes a set exactly with constraints involving only its original variables.
assumptions_latex: S is a subset of a specified finite-dimensional original-variable space.

notation.meaning: constraint system written solely in original variables

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Space Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation whose projection onto original variables equals the modeled set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), an extended-space representation consists of auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and a constraint system \(Q(x,y)\) such that \(S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ Q(x,y)\}\). Equivalently, if \(L=\{(x,y):Q(x,y)\}\), then \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x(L)\). Exactness concerns this projection and does not require a unique auxiliary vector for each \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-space representation introduces auxiliaries and is exact when projecting its feasible set onto the original variables yields the target set.
assumptions_latex: S lies in a specified finite-dimensional original-variable space.
p is a nonnegative integer.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Representation Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength comparison of relaxations after eliminating auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_1\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p_1}\) and \(L_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p_2}\) be extended relaxations of the same set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \(P_i=\operatorname{proj}_x(L_i)\). Representation \(L_1\) is at least as strong as \(L_2\) in original space exactly when \(P_1\subseteq P_2\). It is strictly stronger when the inclusion is strict, and the representations are projection-equivalent when \(P_1=P_2\), irrespective of their auxiliary dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare lifted relaxations through their original-variable projections: smaller projection means stronger, while equal projections mean equivalent strength.
assumptions_latex: S\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(L_i) for i\in\{1,2\}.
Both formulations use the same original-variable space.

notation.meaning: original-variable projection of lifted relaxation i
at least as strong after projection to x-space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected Dominance and Linear Objective Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective characterization and fixed-objective limitation of projected containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If P_1\subseteq P_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n, then for every c\in\mathbb R^n, \inf_{x\in P_1}c^\top x\geq\inf_{x\in P_2}c^\top x. Conversely, for nonempty closed convex P_1 and P_2, this inequality for every c implies P_1\subseteq P_2; under these assumptions strict containment implies strict inequality for at least one c. Strict containment need not improve a specified objective: [0,1]\subsetneq[0,2], but both sets have minimum zero for the objective c=1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected containment gives no-weaker minimization bounds; for nonempty closed convex sets, dominance for every linear objective characterizes containment. A fixed objective may still fail to distinguish strict containment.
assumptions_latex: P_1\subseteq P_2\text{ for the forward implication}.
P_1,P_2\text{ are nonempty, closed, and convex for the converse and strict-separation statements}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_1\subseteq P_2\Rightarrow\forall c,\ \inf_{P_1}c^\top x\geq\inf_{P_2}c^\top x;\quad (P_1,P_2\text{ nonempty closed convex})\Rightarrow\left[P_1\subseteq P_2\iff\forall c,\ \inf_{P_1}c^\top x\geq\inf_{P_2}c^\top x\right]

notation.meaning: linear objective vector in the common original-variable space

knowledge_statements.title: Fortet Pairwise Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-hull linearization of one binary–binary product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary variables \(x_1,x_2\) and a product variable \(w\), the relation \(w=x_1x_2\) is represented exactly by \(w\leq x_1\), \(w\leq x_2\), \(w\geq x_1+x_2-1\), and \(w\geq0\). Moreover, with \(0\leq x_1,x_2\leq1\), these inequalities describe \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x_1,x_2,w)\in\{0,1\}^2\times\mathbb{R}:w=x_1x_2\}\); hence the continuous formulation is ideal for the isolated product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four Fortet inequalities exactly model a binary product and describe the convex hull even when the binary variables are relaxed to the unit interval.
assumptions_latex: x_1,x_2\in\{0,1\} for exact discrete modeling.
w is a continuous auxiliary variable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet Minimality of the Fortet Tetrahedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irredundancy of the isolated binary-product hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polytope \[P=\{(x_1,x_2,w):w\ge0,\ w\le x_1,\ w\le x_2,\ w\ge x_1+x_2-1\}\] is the three-dimensional tetrahedron with vertices \((0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,1)\). Each displayed inequality defines a facet and is irredundant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The four Fortet inequalities are exactly the four facets of the isolated binary-product tetrahedron.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,x_2,w\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,1)\}, and every displayed inequality is facet-defining.
knowledge_statements.title: Facet Minimality of the Fortet Tetrahedron
Complemented Binary-Product Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linearization of a binary variable times a complemented binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\), the complemented product \(z=x(1-y)\) is represented exactly by \(z\leq x\), \(z\leq1-y\), \(z\geq x-y\), and \(z\geq0\). With \(0\leq x,y\leq1\), these inequalities describe the convex hull of the four points satisfying \(z=x(1-y)\). The formulation follows from the Fortet system after substituting the complementary binary variable \(\bar y=1-y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Substituting a complemented binary into the Fortet inequalities gives an ideal linear formulation for the product of a binary and a complement.
assumptions_latex: x,y\in\{0,1\} for the discrete relation.
z is a continuous auxiliary variable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hardness of Optimization over Complete Coupled-Product Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General computational boundary for complete interaction graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational binary-encoded coefficients, linear optimization of \(\sum_i c_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}q_{ij}w_{ij}\) over \(\operatorname{BQP}(K_n)\) is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear optimization over the complete coupled binary-product polytope is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: The coefficients are rational and binary encoded.
The interaction graph may be complete.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence between coupled binary products and cut polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\nabla G\) be obtained from \(G=(V,E)\) by adjoining a vertex \(0\) adjacent to every \(i\in V\). The affine map \[\delta_{0i}=x_i,\qquad \delta_{ij}=x_i+x_j-2w_{ij}\quad(ij\in E)\] maps \(\operatorname{BQP}(G)\) bijectively onto \(\operatorname{CUT}(\nabla G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coupled binary-product polytope is affinely isomorphic to the cut polytope of the suspension graph.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
\(\nabla G\) is its suspension.
knowledge_statements.title: Suspension–Cut Polytope Correspondence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convex hull and basic edgewise relaxation for binary products sharing factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \[\operatorname{BQP}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,w):x\in\{0,1\}^V,\ w_{ij}=x_ix_j\ (ij\in E)\}.\] If \(P_F(G)\) is the intersection of the Fortet systems for all edges, then \(\operatorname{BQP}(G)\subseteq P_F(G)\), possibly strictly. On a triangle, \(x_i=\tfrac12\), \(w_{12}=w_{13}=\tfrac12\), \(w_{23}=0\) belongs to \(P_F(G)\) but violates \(w_{12}+w_{13}-w_{23}\le x_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coupled product polytope is the joint hull of all graph-indexed binary products; independent Fortet blocks can miss inequalities linking several edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph.
Each \(w_{ij}\) represents \(x_ix_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{BQP}(G)\subseteq P_F(G)\), and strict inclusion occurs for a triangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Indexed Coupled Binary-Product Polytope

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forest Exactness of Edgewise Fortet Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclic exactness boundary for coupled product graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(G=(V,E)\) is a forest, then the intersection \(P_F(G)\) of all edgewise Fortet systems satisfies \[P_F(G)=\operatorname{BQP}(G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent Fortet product hulls give the complete coupled hull when the interaction graph is a forest.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite forest.
Every edge has its complete Fortet system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path separation of the odd-subset cycle family in suspension coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For suspension coordinates \(\delta\), build a two-layer graph with states \((v,p)\), \(p\in\{0,1\}\). For every edge \(e=uv\), add parity-preserving copies of cost \(\delta_e\) and parity-switching copies of cost \(1-\delta_e\). The cycle-inequality family is violated exactly when, for some vertex \(r\), the shortest-path distance from \((r,0)\) to \((r,1)\) is less than \(1\). Thus all cycle inequalities can be separated by polynomially many shortest-path computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd-subset cycle inequalities are separated in polynomial time by shortest paths in a two-layer parity graph.
assumptions_latex: The suspension graph is finite.
The candidate coordinates are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Cycle-inequality separation is polynomial in the graph size and input bit length.}

notation.meaning: vertex v with accumulated subset parity p
suspension cut coordinate of edge e

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Separation of Cycle Inequalities

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle Inequalities for Coupled Binary Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical cyclic inequalities transferred through the suspension–cut correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=\nabla G\), with \(\delta_{0i}=x_i\) and \(\delta_{ij}=x_i+x_j-2w_{ij}\). For every simple cycle \(C\) of \(H\) and every odd-cardinality subset \(F\subseteq E(C)\), every point of \(\operatorname{BQP}(G)\) satisfies
\[\sum_{e\in F}\delta_e-\sum_{e\in E(C)\setminus F}\delta_e\le |F|-1.\]
Substitution gives a valid linear coupling inequality in \((x,w)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every odd-subset cycle inequality of the suspension cut polytope transfers to a valid inequality coupling binary-product variables.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph.
\(C\) is a simple cycle of \(\nabla G\).
\(|F|\) is odd.

notation.meaning: odd subset of the selected cycle edges

Coupled Binary-Product Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convex hull for multiple binary products sharing variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), the coupled binary-product polytope is \(\operatorname{BQP}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,w):x\in\{0,1\}^{V},\ w_{ij}=x_ix_j\text{ for }ij\in E\}\). Intersecting the Fortet inequalities separately over all edges produces a relaxation \(P_F(G)\) satisfying \(\operatorname{BQP}(G)\subseteq P_F(G)\), but the inclusion can be strict. For a triangle, \(x_i=1/2\), \(w_{12}=w_{13}=1/2\), and \(w_{23}=0\) satisfies every pairwise Fortet system but violates the valid coupling inequality \(w_{12}+w_{13}-w_{23}\leq x_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The joint product polytope is the convex hull of all coupled binary products; edgewise Fortet constraints can miss inequalities linking several products.
assumptions_latex: G is a finite simple graph.
Each edge variable w_{ij} represents x_ix_j.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Bounded Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull formulation for a binary product with a nonnegative bounded continuous factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(0\le x\le U\), and \(U<\infty\). The graph of \(w=bx\) has the ideal linear extended formulation
\[
0\le w\le Ub,\qquad w\le x,\qquad w\ge x-U(1-b).
\]
For binary \(b\), these inequalities imply \(w=0\) when \(b=0\) and \(w=x\) when \(b=1\). After relaxing \(b\in[0,1]\), they describe the convex hull of \(\{(b,x,w):b\in\{0,1\},\ 0\le x\le U,\ w=bx\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four linear inequalities exactly model a binary variable times a nonnegative bounded factor and remain convex-hull exact after relaxing the binary variable.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le x\le U<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w=bx\) for integral \(b\), and the relaxation is the convex hull of the product graph.

Sign-Crossing Bounded Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull formulation when the continuous factor has finite bounds of opposite signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(L\le x\le U\), and \(L<0<U\). The graph of \(w=bx\) is represented by
\[
Lb\le w\le Ub,
\qquad
x-U(1-b)\le w\le x-L(1-b).
\]
For binary \(b\), the first pair forces \(w=0\) at \(b=0\), while the second pair forces \(w=x\) at \(b=1\). With \(0\le b\le1\), the four inequalities describe the convex hull of the bounded binary–continuous product graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four bound-derived inequalities give the exact convex hull of a binary product whose continuous factor can be positive or negative.
assumptions_latex: \(-\infty<L<0<U<\infty\)
\(L\le x\le U\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w=bx\) for integral \(b\), with a convex-hull-exact continuous relaxation.

notation.meaning: finite lower and upper bounds crossing zero

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Ideality Under Loose Crossing Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference between binary exactness and hull strength when non-tight bounds are substituted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the true domain is \(L\le x\le U\) with \(L<0<U\), but the product inequalities use valid looser bounds \(\ell\le L\) and \(u\ge U\). The system remains exact for binary \(b\), but its continuous relaxation need not be the true hull. For \(x\in[-1,1]\) with substituted bounds \([-2,2]\), \((b,x,w)=(\tfrac12,0,1)\) satisfies the substituted-bound inequalities, whereas the true hull requires \(w\le b=\tfrac12\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loose valid crossing bounds preserve binary exactness but can destroy ideality.
assumptions_latex: \(L<0<U\) are the true interval endpoints.
\(\ell\le L\) and \(u\ge U\) are finite valid substituted bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The loose-bound relaxation may strictly contain the true product hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary–Linear-Function Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Glover formulation for multiplying a bounded affine function by a binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x)=a^{\mathsf T}x+c\) satisfy valid finite bounds \(L\le g(x)\le U\) on a domain \(X\), and let \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Introducing \(w\) for \(b g(x)\), impose
\[
Lb\le w\le Ub,
\qquad
g(x)-U(1-b)\le w\le g(x)-L(1-b).
\]
These linear inequalities are equivalent to \(w=b g(x)\) for integral \(b\). If the only restriction on the scalar image \(g(x)\) is its interval bound, relaxing \(b\) yields the convex hull in \((b,g(x),w)\)-space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid bounds on an affine function produce four linear inequalities that exactly model its product with a binary variable.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\) and \(g(x)=a^{\mathsf T}x+c\)
\(L\le g(x)\le U\) with finite \(L,U\)

notation.meaning: valid bounds on the affine function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar-Hull Ideality Does Not Imply Original-Space Ideality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the Glover formulation when the affine factor aggregates several variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even with exact bounds \(L=\min_Xg\) and \(U=\max_Xg\), the four scalar Glover inequalities need not describe \(\operatorname{conv}\{(b,x,w):b\in\{0,1\},\ x\in X,\ w=bg(x)\}\) in full \((b,x,w)\)-space. For \(X=[0,1]^2\), \(g(x)=x_1+x_2\), and \((L,U)=(0,2)\), the point \((b,x_1,x_2,w)=(\tfrac12,1,0,1)\) satisfies the Glover inequalities but is outside that convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tight scalar bounds give the aggregated product hull, but they do not generally make the formulation ideal in the original variable space.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in[0,1]\), \(x\in X\), and exact scalar bounds on \(g(X)\) are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scalar-image ideality does not generally imply ideality in \((b,x,w)\)-space.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar-Hull Ideality Does Not Imply Original-Space Ideality
Sign-Dependent Glover Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplified Glover inequalities when a bounded affine factor has a known sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b\in\{0,1\}\) and let \(g(x)\) be affine. If \(0\le g(x)\le U\), then \(w=b g(x)\) is represented by
\[
0\le w\le Ub,\qquad w\le g(x),\qquad w\ge g(x)-U(1-b).
\]
If instead \(L\le g(x)\le0\), it is represented by
\[
Lb\le w\le0,\qquad w\ge g(x),\qquad w\le g(x)-L(1-b).
\]
Each system remains the convex hull in \((b,g(x),w)\)-space after replacing binary membership by \(0\le b\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Known nonnegativity or nonpositivity removes sign-crossing terms and yields specialized convex-hull formulations for binary–affine products.
assumptions_latex: Either \(0\le g(x)\le U\) or \(L\le g(x)\le0\)
\(L,U\) are finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w=b g(x)\), with the displayed sign-specific relaxation equal to the scalar product hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-or-Interval Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard positive semicontinuous domain and its binary extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constants \(0<L\le U<\infty\), a scalar variable \(x\) has a zero-or-interval, or positive semicontinuous, domain when
\[
x\in\{0\}\cup[L,U].
\]
Equivalently, there exists \(b\in\{0,1\}\) such that
\[
Lb\le x\le Ub.
\]
Under this formulation, \(b=0\) forces \(x=0\), whereas \(b=1\) restricts \(x\) to \([L,U]\). Because \(L>0\), every nonzero feasible value activates the binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive semicontinuous variable is either zero or lies in a positive bounded interval; one binary variable gives an equivalent formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(0<L\le U<\infty\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected Convex Hull of a Positive Zero-or-Interval Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex geometry after eliminating the activation indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(0<L\le U\) and \(D=\{0\}\cup[L,U]\), then
\[
\operatorname{conv}(D)=[0,U].
\]
Thus scalar convexification fills the gap \((0,L)\); retaining the minimum active level requires discrete or extended-formulation information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar convex hull is the full interval from zero to the upper bound, so convexification erases the minimum active level.
assumptions_latex: \(0<L\le U<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Convex Hull of a Positive Zero-or-Interval Domain
Binary Activation Links
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear linking conditions connecting an activity indicator to a semicontinuous variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(0<L\le U\), and impose
\[
Lb\le x\le Ub.
\]
These are binary activation links: \(b=0\) implies \(x=0\), and \(b=1\) implies \(L\le x\le U\). Conversely, every \(x\in\{0\}\cup[L,U]\) admits exactly one compatible value of \(b\). If a fixed charge \(f\ge0\) is incurred upon activation, the linear objective term \(fb\) charges zero at \(x=0\) and \(f\) at every feasible nonzero value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower and upper binary links enforce inactivity at zero, an active operating interval, and an optional fixed charge whenever activity occurs.
assumptions_latex: \(0<L\le U<\infty\)
\(f\ge0\) when a fixed charge is modeled
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Lb\le x\le Ub\) enforces \(b=0\iff x=0\) and \(b=1\iff x\in[L,U]\).

Unary Value Disaggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact unary disaggregation of a bounded integer–continuous product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\), \(L\le x\le U\), and \(y=nx\). Introduce \(\delta_k\in\{0,1\}\) and \(z_k\) for \(k=0,\ldots,N\), with
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N}\delta_k=1,
\qquad n=\sum_{k=0}^{N}k\delta_k,
\qquad y=\sum_{k=0}^{N}kz_k.
\]
For every \(k\), impose the bounded binary-product hull
\[
L\delta_k\le z_k\le U\delta_k,
\qquad x-U(1-\delta_k)\le z_k\le x-L(1-\delta_k).
\]
Then \(z_k=\delta_kx\), so the formulation is exactly equivalent to \(y=nx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-hot encoding of each integer value, coupled with binary-product hulls, gives an exact linear formulation of an integer–continuous product.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\)
\(L\le x\le U\) with finite bounds
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=nx\) is equivalent to the displayed mixed-integer linear extended formulation.

notation.meaning: indicator that the integer equals k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-size cost of explicitly enumerating every attainable integer value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\), the displayed unary value-disaggregation template uses \(N+1\) binary selectors and \(N+1\) product auxiliaries, with \(O(N)\) linear rows. Its size is linear in \(N\) but can be exponential in the binary encoding length \(\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary value disaggregation has linear size in the number of integer values and is generally pseudo-polynomial in the bit length of the bound.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) is a nonnegative integer encoded in binary.
Every value from \(0\) through \(N\) is represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}=O(N),\quad\text{which is not generally polynomial in }\log N.
knowledge_statements.title: Unary Disaggregation Size
Radix-Expansion Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary-radix expansion of a bounded integer–continuous product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\), \(m=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\), and \(L\le x\le U\). Introduce bits \(b_j\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[
n=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^j b_j,
\]
with \(n\le N\), and variables \(z_j=b_jx\). Represent each \(z_j\) by
\[
Lb_j\le z_j\le Ub_j,
\qquad x-U(1-b_j)\le z_j\le x-L(1-b_j).
\]
Then the integer–continuous product is exactly
\[
y=nx=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jz_j.
\]
Thus binary radix expansion requires only logarithmically many product variables and binary digits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary expansion reduces an exact bounded integer–continuous product formulation to logarithmically many binary–continuous product hulls.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\)
\(L\le x\le U\) with finite bounds
\(m=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessity of the Radix Range Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness failure for a non-power-of-two domain cardinality when unused bit patterns are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the intended domain \(n\in\{0,1,\ldots,5\}\), three bits are required, but the unrestricted equation
\[
n=b_0+2b_1+4b_2,
\qquad b\in\{0,1\}^3,
\]
admits \(b=(0,1,1)\), giving \(n=6\), and \(b=(1,1,1)\), giving \(n=7\). Hence the formulation is not exact unless \(n\le5\), or an equivalent restriction excluding unused patterns, is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a non-power-of-two range, unrestricted radix bits create invalid integer values, so the range cap is essential.
assumptions_latex: The intended domain is \(\{0,1,\ldots,5\}\)
Three unrestricted binary digits are used
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unrestricted encoding admits the spurious values \(6\) and \(7\).
knowledge_statements.title: Necessity of the Radix Range Restriction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact radix linearization for a finite integer interval with a nonzero lower endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\{\ell,\ell+1,\ldots,u\}\), set \(N=u-\ell\) and \(m=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\), and let \(L\le x\le U\). Impose
\[
n=\ell+�sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jb_j,
\qquad \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jb_j\le N,
\qquad b_j\in\{0,1\}.
\]
If \(z_j=b_jx\) is represented by the binary–continuous product hull, then
\[
y=\ell x+�sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jz_j
\]
represents \(y=nx\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating the integer range to start at zero extends binary-radix product linearization to every finite integer interval.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z\) with \(\ell\le u\)
\(L\le x\le U\) with finite bounds
Each \(z_j=b_jx\) is represented exactly

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spurious values produced by an unrestricted partially filled final block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the intended domain \(n\in\{0,\ldots,5\}\), choose block size \(B=4\). The hybrid expression
\[
n=4\delta_1+b_0+2b_1,
\qquad \delta_0+�delta_1=1,
\]
without the cap \(n\le5\) admits \(\delta_1=1\) and \((b_0,b_1)=(0,1)\) or \((1,1)\), producing the spurious values \(6\) and \(7\). Thus a truncated final block requires an explicit range restriction or an equivalent conditional restriction on its offset digits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the last hybrid block is only partially filled, unrestricted offset bits create values outside the intended integer domain.
assumptions_latex: The intended integer domain is \(\{0,\ldots,5\}\)
Block size is \(B=4\)
No final range cap or equivalent tail restriction is imposed

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted and Truncated Hybrid Integer Disaggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact block-unary and within-block radix formulation for an arbitrary finite integer interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\{\ell,\ldots,u\}\), \(N=u-\ell\), choose \(B=2^m\), and set \(Q=\lfloor N/B\rfloor\). Introduce \(\delta_q\in\{0,1\}\) for \(q=0,\ldots,Q\) and \(b_j\in\{0,1\}\) for \(j=0,�ldots,m-1\), with
\[
\sum_{q=0}^{Q}\delta_q=1,
\qquad n-\ell=B\sum_{q=0}^{Q}q\delta_q+�sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jb_j,
\qquad n\le u.
\]
For finite \(L\le x\le U\), represent \(z_q=\delta_qx\) and \(v_j=b_jx\) by their binary–continuous product hulls. Then
\[
y=\ell x+B\sum_{q=0}^{Q}qz_q+�sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jv_j
\]
represents \(y=nx\) exactly. The construction uses \(Q+1+m\) binary selectors and the same number of product auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unary block selector plus binary within-block digits exactly linearizes an integer–continuous product on any shifted finite range, including a truncated final block.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z\) with \(\ell\le u\)
\(B=2^m\) with \(m\ge0\)
\(L\le x\le U\) with finite bounds
Every selector product is represented exactly

Hybrid Integer Disaggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact product formulation combining unary block selection with binary within-block digits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=2^m\), \(n\in\{0,\ldots,(Q+1)B-1\}\), and \(L\le x\le U\). Write
\[
n=B\sum_{q=0}^{Q}q\delta_q+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jb_j,
\qquad \sum_{q=0}^{Q}\delta_q=1,
\]
where \(\delta_q,b_j\in\{0,1\}\). Introduce \(z_q=\delta_qx\) and \(v_j=b_jx\), representing every binary–continuous product by its four bound inequalities. Then
\[
y=B\sum_{q=0}^{Q}qz_q+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}2^jv_j
\]
is exactly equal to \(nx\). The block size \(B\) controls the tradeoff between unary indicators and radix digits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block index encoded unary and an offset encoded in binary yield an exact tunable formulation of a bounded integer–continuous product.
assumptions_latex: \(B=2^m\) and \(Q,m\) are nonnegative integers
\(L\le x\le U\) with finite bounds
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=nx\) under the displayed hybrid unary–radix disaggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Factor Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact integer–integer product formulation obtained by expanding one bounded factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\), \(m\in\{0,\ldots,M\}\), and \(p=nm\). Introduce one-hot variables \(\delta_k\in\{0,1\}\) with
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N}\delta_k=1,
\qquad n=\sum_{k=0}^{N}k\delta_k.
\]
For \(z_k=\delta_km\), impose
\[
0\le z_k\le M\delta_k,
\qquad z_k\le m,
\qquad z_k\ge m-M(1-\delta_k).
\]
The single-factor expansion
\[
p=\sum_{k=0}^{N}kz_k
\]
is then exactly equivalent to \(p=nm\). Only the factor \(n\) is disaggregated; integrality of \(m\) is retained separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding one integer factor into one-hot values converts an integer–integer product into exact binary–bounded-integer product links.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\)
\(m\in\{0,\ldots,M\}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\) and \(m\in\{0,\ldots,M\}\), expanding \(n\) with the displayed template uses \(N+1\) selectors and \(N+1\) product auxiliaries, whereas expanding \(m\) uses \(M+1\) of each. Two-Factor Disaggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact joint-value disaggregation for a product of two bounded nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\) and \(m\in\{0,\ldots,M\}\). Introduce one-hot variables \(\delta_i,\varepsilon_j\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{N}\delta_i=1,
\qquad
\sum_{j=0}^{M}\varepsilon_j=1,
\]
and joint indicators \(\lambda_{ij}\ge0\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{M}\lambda_{ij}=\delta_i,
\qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{N}\lambda_{ij}=\varepsilon_j.
\]
With \(n=\sum_i i\delta_i\), \(m=\sum_jj\varepsilon_j\), and
\[
p=\sum_{i=0}^{N}\sum_{j=0}^{M}ij\lambda_{ij},
\]
the one-hot conditions force exactly one joint indicator to equal one, and hence \(p=nm\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint one-hot disaggregation selects one value pair and computes the integer product as a linear weighted sum over that pair.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\)
\(m\in\{0,\ldots,M\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=nm\) in the displayed joint disaggregation formulation.

notation.meaning: one-hot indicators for the two integer factors

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unary, Radix, and Joint-Value Resource Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-specific variable and row growth under a fixed termwise product-linearization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\) and put \(m=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\). One-hot value disaggregation uses \(N+1\) indicators and \(N+1\) associated product auxiliaries, with a constant number of rows per value, hence \(\Theta(N+1)\) encoding-specific variables and rows. Binary-radix expansion uses \(m\) bits and \(m\) product auxiliaries, with a constant number of rows per bit plus the range cap, hence \(\Theta(m)=\Theta(\log(N+1))\) variables and rows. For two ranges of cardinalities \(N+1\) and \(M+1\), full joint-value disaggregation uses \((N+1)(M+1)\) joint indicators and \(\Theta((N+1)(M+1))\) encoding-specific rows. These counts do not identify total binary description length, which also includes positional and value coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary, binary-radix, and full joint-value encodings have linear-in-range, logarithmic-in-range, and product-of-cardinalities variable-and-row growth, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \(N,M\) are nonnegative integers
Each binary–bounded product is represented with a constant number of rows
Unchanged surrounding-model components are excluded

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource convention for comparing bounded-integer product encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed written extended formulation \(F\), define its encoding-size vector by
\[
\sigma(F)=(n_{\mathrm{bin}},n_{\mathrm{aux}},n_{\mathrm{row}},\ell_{\mathrm{data}}),
\]
where the components count encoding-specific binary variables, other auxiliary variables, scalar linear rows, and the total binary length of the rational coefficients and indices. Constraints and variables inherited unchanged from the surrounding model are excluded. Comparisons must either use this vector componentwise or declare a scalar aggregation of its components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding size is presentation-specific and should distinguish binary variables, other auxiliaries, linear rows, and coefficient-data bit length.
assumptions_latex: A concrete finite rational MILP presentation is fixed
Inherited model components are identified and excluded consistently
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(F)=(n_{\mathrm{bin}},n_{\mathrm{aux}},n_{\mathrm{row}},\ell_{\mathrm{data}})\) supplies an unambiguous local size convention.

notation.meaning: binary length of rational data and indices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variable Count Does Not Determine Bit Encoding Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between combinatorial formulation counts and total binary description size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two formulations with the same numbers of variables and rows can have different \(\ell_{\mathrm{data}}\) because coefficient magnitudes and index representations contribute to binary length. In particular, radix weights \(2^j\) require \(j+1\) magnitude bits even though each weight occurs in a formulation with only logarithmically many digit variables. Therefore a bound on variable-and-row count alone is not a bound on total binary encoding length unless coefficient bit lengths are also controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few variables and constraints do not by themselves imply a small binary description, because coefficient magnitudes also consume bits.
assumptions_latex: Rational coefficients are written in binary
Total description size includes coefficient data

These counts concern exact MILP extended formulations, excluding constraints inherited from the surrounding model.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares extended LP relaxations after projection onto common original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be exact integer encodings of the same bounded-integer product set, and let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be their continuous linear relaxations. If \(\pi\) projects each extended formulation onto the common original variables and product variable, then \(E_1\) is at least as strong as \(E_2\) precisely when \[\pi(P_1)\subseteq \pi(P_2).\] For every linear objective expressed in the projected variables, minimization over \(P_1\) then gives a lower bound no weaker than minimization over \(P_2\). Equality of the projected sets means equal relaxation strength under this comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One encoding is stronger when its projected LP relaxation is contained in the other's, producing at least as strong a bound for every common linear objective.
assumptions_latex: \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) represent the same integer feasible set.
Both relaxations are projected onto identical original and product variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of universal bound ordering for incomparable projected convex relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_1,P_2\subset\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty compact convex projected relaxations. If neither \(P_1\subseteq P_2\) nor \(P_2\subseteq P_1\), then there exist \(c,d\in\mathbb R^d\) such that
\[
\min_{x\in P_1}c^Tx<\min_{x\in P_2}c^Tx,
\qquad
\min_{x\in P_2}d^Tx<\min_{x\in P_1}d^Tx.
\]
Thus neither formulation supplies a universally stronger minimization bound over all common linear objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For incomparable projected relaxations, each can be stronger for some linear objective, so neither universally dominates.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,P_2\) are nonempty compact convex sets in the same space
Neither set contains the other
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projected-set incomparability implies objective-dependent rather than universal relaxation strength.

notation.meaning: linear objective vectors witnessing opposite orderings

knowledge_statements.title: Incomparable Projections Give Objective-Dependent Strength
Branching Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines compatibility between an integer encoding and a prescribed branching family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=\phi(u)\) be an exact encoding of a bounded integer variable using binary variables \(u\), and let \(\mathcal D\) be a family of exhaustive disjunctions on \(x\). The encoding is branching-compatible with \(\mathcal D\) if, for every \(D=\bigvee_{r=1}^q\{x\in X_r\}\) in \(\mathcal D\), there exist faces \(F_r\) of the encoded binary set, each obtained by fixing designated components of \(u\), such that \[\{u:\phi(u)\in X_r\}=F_r\quad(r=1,\ldots,q),\qquad \bigcup_{r=1}^qF_r=\{u:\phi(u)\text{ is feasible}\}.\] Thus the original-variable branch is realized exactly without additional linking inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding is branching-compatible when every prescribed branch on the integer variable is represented exactly by fixing designated encoding bits.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is exact on the feasible binary encodings.
Every disjunction in \(\mathcal D\) is exhaustive on the integer domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each branch disjunction corresponds exactly to a union of encoding faces.

notation.meaning: map from encoding bits to the integer value
face produced by fixing encoding variables

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Binary-Monomial Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal extended formulation for one multilinear monomial of binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty index set \(S\), binary variables \(x_i\), and an auxiliary variable \(y_S\), the identity \(y_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) is represented by \[0\le y_S\le 1,\qquad y_S\le x_i\quad(i\in S),\qquad y_S\ge \sum_{i\in S}x_i-|S|+1.\] With \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), these inequalities force the product identity. If instead \(0\le x_i\le1\), the displayed system is the convex hull of \(\{(x,y_S):x\in\{0,1\}^{S},\ y_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary monomial is linearized directly by one auxiliary, upper bounds from every factor, and one aggregate lower bound; the formulation is ideal.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and nonempty.
\(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) for exactness, or \(x_i\in[0,1]\) for the hull statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities give an exact and ideal formulation of \(y_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Binary-Monomial Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a binary monomial through a tree of pairwise products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input binary factors \(x_i\) indexed by a finite set \(S\) and choose a rooted binary tree whose leaves are those factors. For every internal node with child values \(a,b\), introduce \(v\) and impose \[v\le a,\qquad v\le b,\qquad v\ge a+b-1,\qquad v\ge0.\] Process internal nodes from the leaves toward the root, reusing each child variable in its parent constraint. With binary leaves, every internal value equals the product of its descendant leaves; output the root variable as \(y_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\). The chosen tree determines the extended relaxation when these constraints interact with the surrounding model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build a monomial through a binary tree, applying the exact two-factor binary-product formulation at every internal node and returning the root variable.
assumptions_latex: \(|S|\ge2\) and every leaf variable is binary.
The factorization structure is a rooted binary tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root variable equals \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) at every integer-feasible point.

notation.meaning: auxiliary value at an internal tree node

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(c>0\) and the same expression \(\min_{y\in\{0,1\}}(-c)y(d-1-\sum_i x_i)\) is used, then at \(x=0\) its value is \(-c(d-1)<0\), whereas \(c\prod_i x_i=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sign-specific quadratization of a negatively weighted binary monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge2\), \(x\in\{0,1\}^d\), and \(c<0\), \[c\prod_{i=1}^d x_i=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}}(-c)y\left(d-1-\sum_{i=1}^d x_i\right).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Penalty Threshold for the Positive Rosenberg Chain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp sufficient threshold and failure of an undersized product-enforcement penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the positive-chain quadratization, \(M\ge c\) is sufficient for equality of minimum values. The threshold cannot be reduced uniformly: for \(d=3\), \(x=(1,1,1)\), and \(0<M<c\), choosing \(y_1=0\) gives value \(M<c=cx_1x_2x_3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Rosenberg-chain penalty must be at least the positive monomial coefficient; an undersized penalty makes the quadratization inexact.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Threshold for the Positive Rosenberg Chain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quadratic minimization representation for a positively weighted binary monomial using partial-product auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\ge3\), \(c>0\), and \(x\in\{0,1\}^d\). Introduce \(y_1,\ldots,y_{d-2}\in\{0,1\}\), set \(a_1=x_1,b_1=x_2\), and for \(k\ge2\) set \(a_k=y_{k-1},b_k=x_{k+1}\). With \(P(a,b,y)=ab-2ay-2by+3y\), every \(M\ge c\) satisfies
\[c\prod_{i=1}^d x_i=\min_y\left(cy_{d-2}x_d+M\sum_{k=1}^{d-2}P(a_k,b_k,y_k)\right).\]
For \(d=2\), the monomial is already quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive binary monomial admits an exact Rosenberg-chain quadratization with d−2 partial-product auxiliaries and a penalty at least as large as its coefficient.
assumptions_latex: \(c>0\) and \(M\ge c\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative Rosenberg penalty that vanishes when y=ab
auxiliary for a successive partial product

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Monomial Rosenberg Chain Quadratization
Sign-Sensitive Quadratizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-auxiliary quadratization identity for a negatively weighted binary monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge2\), \(x\in\{0,1\}^d\), and \(c<0\), the negative monomial has the exact quadratization \[c\prod_{i=1}^d x_i=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}}(-c)y\left(d-1-\sum_{i=1}^d x_i\right).\] If all factors equal one, the coefficient of \(y\) on the right is \(c<0\), so minimization selects \(y=1\). Otherwise that coefficient is nonnegative and \(y=0\) attains zero. Consequently, quadratization templates must respect the coefficient sign: multiplying this identity by a negative scalar preserves minimization equivalence, whereas using it for a positive monomial does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative binary monomial admits an exact one-auxiliary quadratic minimization identity; reversing its coefficient sign invalidates the same template.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed quadratic function minimizes exactly to \(c\prod_{i=1}^d x_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed negative-monomial identity is mathematically plausible, but the specialized sign-sensitive quadratization has no source locator. The explanatory case analysis is also proof text and should be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Auxiliary Quadratizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact quadratization with auxiliaries reused across multiple higher-order terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb R\) be a pseudo-Boolean polynomial with several higher-order monomials. A shared-auxiliary quadratization of \(f\) is a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function \(Q:\{0,1\}^{n+m}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[f(x)=\min_{z\in\{0,1\}^m}Q(x,z)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\{0,1\}^n,\] where at least one component of \(z\) occurs in quadratic terms associated with more than one original monomial. Sharing is exact only when the minimizing assignments of the reused auxiliaries yield the stated equality for every fixed \(x\); termwise exact identities alone do not establish this compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared-auxiliary quadratization is an exact quadratic minimization representation in which at least one auxiliary participates in representing multiple original monomials.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a pseudo-Boolean polynomial.
\(Q\) has total degree at most two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness requires \(f(x)=\min_z Q(x,z)\) simultaneously for every binary \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimization identity is a standard quadratization condition, but the additional criterion defining when an auxiliary is shared across original monomials is specialized and requires an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sign Box Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick hull on a nondegenerate box whose factor intervals each have one sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and suppose both intervals are nondegenerate and neither has an interior sign change. The convex hull of \(w=xy\) over this box is given by \[w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\qquad w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y,\] \[w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\qquad w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y.\] These four planes interpolate the product at the box corners. The one-sign assumption affects their slopes and intercepts but does not alter the hull formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On nondegenerate one-sign factor intervals, the four McCormick inequalities give the exact convex hull of a bilinear graph.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\).
Each interval lies wholly in one closed half-line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four displayed inequalities describe \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy)\}\) over the box.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick hull when at least one factor interval crosses zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), with nondegenerate intervals and at least one strict sign crossing, such as \(\ell_x<0<u_x\). The convex hull of \(w=xy\) is given by \[w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\qquad w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y,\] \[w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\qquad w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y.\] Thus a sign partition is not required for validity or hull exactness on this single box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same four McCormick inequalities describe the exact bilinear hull on a mixed-sign box; no sign partition is required for this hull description.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\).
At least one interval contains both negative and positive values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system equals the convex hull of the bilinear graph on the mixed-sign box.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Box Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse of the bilinear hull when one or both factor intervals are singletons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and \(w=xy\). If \(\ell_x=u_x=\bar x\), then the graph and its convex hull satisfy the affine relations \[x=\bar x,\qquad w=\bar x y,\qquad y\in[\ell_y,u_y].\] Symmetrically, if \(\ell_y=u_y=\bar y\), then \(y=\bar y\) and \(w=\bar yx\). If both intervals are singletons, the hull is the single point \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar x\bar y)\). Substitution into the four McCormick inequalities reduces them to these equalities, so redundant duplicate inequalities may be removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a factor is fixed, its bilinear product becomes affine; when both factors are fixed, the hull is a single point.
assumptions_latex: At least one factor interval is a singleton.
All bounds are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bilinear hull collapses to an affine segment or a single point.

knowledge_statements.title: Underestimating Envelope Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two affine lower facets of the bilinear convex envelope on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite bounds \(\ell_x<u_x\), \(\ell_y<u_y\), every point of the bilinear graph \(w=xy\) satisfies the two affine underestimators \[w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\qquad w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y.\] Their pointwise maximum is the convex envelope of \(xy\) on the rectangle: \[\operatorname{vex}(xy)=\max\{\ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\qquad u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y\}.\] In the three-dimensional convex hull, each inequality is tight at three box-corner graph points and defines a lower hull facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope of a bilinear term is the maximum of two affine underestimators, each defining a lower hull facet through three corner graph points.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\).
The domain is the rectangle \([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum of the two lower planes is \(\operatorname{vex}(xy)\).

notation.meaning: convex envelope of the bilinear function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corner incidence and switching locus of the two affine underestimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(x-\ell_x)/(u_x-\ell_x)\) and \(Y=(y-\ell_y)/(u_y-\ell_y)\). The lower plane \(L_1=\ell_xy+\ell_yx-\ell_x\ell_y\) is exact on the graph whenever \(x=\ell_x\) or \(y=\ell_y\), while \(L_2=u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y\) is exact whenever \(x=u_x\) or \(y=u_y\). Moreover, \(L_1=L_2\) exactly when \(X+Y=1\). Thus the facets meet along the lifted antidiagonal joining \((\ell_x,u_y,\ell_xu_y)\) and \((u_x,\ell_y,u_x\ell_y)\), and each plane is active on one side of that antidiagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower McCormick facets have complementary three-corner incidence and switch across the normalized antidiagonal X+Y=1.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\).
\((x,y)\in[\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\).

knowledge_statements.title: Overestimating Envelope Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two affine upper facets of the bilinear concave envelope on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite bounds \(\ell_x<u_x\), \(\ell_y<u_y\), every point of the bilinear graph \(w=xy\) satisfies the two affine overestimators \[w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\qquad w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y.\] Their pointwise minimum is the concave envelope of \(xy\) on the rectangle: \[\operatorname{cav}(xy)=\min\{u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\qquad \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y\}.\] In the three-dimensional convex hull, each inequality is tight at three box-corner graph points and defines an upper hull facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The concave envelope of a bilinear term is the minimum of two affine overestimators, each defining an upper hull facet through three corner graph points.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\).
The domain is the rectangle \([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum of the two upper planes is \(\operatorname{cav}(xy)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope-Side Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-reversal correspondence between lower and upper bilinear envelope facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the transformation \(y'=-y\), \(w'=-w\), which maps \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\) to \(y'\in[-u_y,-\ell_y]\) and preserves the graph relation through \(w'=xy'\). Under this bijection, every valid lower inequality \[w'\ge a x+b y'+c\] becomes the valid upper inequality \[w\le -a x+b y-c.\] Applying the transformation to the two McCormick underestimating facets yields exactly the two overestimating facets on the original box, and applying it again restores the lower pair. Hence the convex and concave envelope sides are interchanged by reversing one factor and the product coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating one factor and the product maps lower McCormick facets bijectively to upper facets, revealing symmetry between the two envelope sides.
assumptions_latex: All factor bounds are finite.
The transformation updates the negated factor bounds to \([-u_y,-\ell_y]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \((x,y,w)\mapsto(x,-y,-w)\) exchanges underestimating and overestimating facets.

notation.meaning: coefficients of an affine supporting plane

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Dependent Envelope Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity and worst-case error of McCormick envelopes under rectangular bound tightening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=[\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\) and let \(M(B)=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,w):(x,y)\in B,\ w=xy\}\), represented by the four McCormick inequalities. If \(B'\subseteq B\) is another rectangle, then \[M(B')\subseteq M(B)\cap(B'\times\mathbb R).\] Thus tightening either factor interval cannot weaken the relaxation. Moreover, on \(B\), the maximum vertical deviation of either McCormick envelope from \(xy\) is \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\); hence this error tends to zero when either interval width tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: McCormick relaxations become no weaker as factor bounds tighten, and their maximum one-sided product error equals one quarter of the product of the interval widths.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\).
\(B'\subseteq B\) is rectangular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(B')\subseteq M(B)\cap(B'\times\mathbb R)\), with one-sided error at most \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\).

notation.meaning: McCormick hull of the bilinear graph over box B

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for constructing and quantifying bound-dependent McCormick envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard four-plane McCormick construction and its finite error constant require finite valid endpoints \(\ell_x,u_x,\ell_y,u_y\) containing the intended factor domain. If a required endpoint is infinite, the corresponding finite plane and the bound \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\) are unavailable in this form. If an asserted interval excludes a feasible factor value, the resulting inequalities need not contain the original bilinear graph and therefore need not be a valid relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite containing bounds are required for the standard four-plane envelope and finite error estimate; an invalid bound can invalidate the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The intended graph is \(\{(x,y,xy):(x,y)\in D\}\).
The McCormick planes are formed from asserted interval endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\subseteq[\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\text{ with finite endpoints is required for the stated construction and error bound.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite and Valid Bound Requirement
One-Factor Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive McCormick relaxation obtained by partitioning one factor interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \([\ell_x,u_x]\) into intervals \(I_k=[a_{k-1},a_k]\), \(k=1,\ldots,K\), while retaining \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\). The one-factor partitioned relaxation is the mixed-integer disjunction \[\sum_{k=1}^K\delta_k=1,\qquad \delta_k\in\{0,1\},\qquad \delta_k=1\ \Longrightarrow\ (x,y,w)\in M(I_k\times[\ell_y,u_y]).\] Its projection is \(\bigcup_{k=1}^K M(I_k\times[\ell_y,u_y])\), contains every point satisfying \(w=xy\), and is contained in the unpartitioned relaxation \(M([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y])\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select one interval for one factor and impose its local McCormick envelope. The resulting disjunctive relaxation is valid and at least as strong as the global envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_K=u_x\).
\(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\).

notation.meaning: k-th interval of the partition of the x-domain
McCormick hull over the indicated rectangle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp error bound and refinement behavior when only one factor domain is partitioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{I_k\}_{k=1}^K\) partition \([\ell_x,u_x]\), let \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and let \(R=\bigcup_kM(I_k\times[\ell_y,u_y])\). Then \[\sup_{(x,y,w)\in R}|w-xy|=\frac{u_y-\ell_y}{4}\max_k\operatorname{width}(I_k).\] Refining the partition can only shrink \(R\). Hence nested partitions converge uniformly to \(w=xy\) when their maximum interval width tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sharp error is one quarter of the unpartitioned-factor width times the largest partition interval width; it vanishes with the partition mesh.
assumptions_latex: Both factor domains are bounded intervals.
\(\{I_k\}\) is an exhaustive interval partition of the x-domain.

notation.meaning: mesh size of the partitioned factor

knowledge_statements.title: One-Factor Mesh Error and Convergence
Two-Factor Grid Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive McCormick relaxation over a Cartesian grid of factor intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{I_i\}_{i=1}^P\) partition \([\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(\{J_j\}_{j=1}^Q\) partition \([\ell_y,u_y]\). The two-factor grid relaxation selects exactly one cell and imposes its local envelope: \[\sum_{i=1}^P\sum_{j=1}^Q\delta_{ij}=1,\qquad \delta_{ij}\in\{0,1\},\qquad \delta_{ij}=1\ \Longrightarrow\ (x,y,w)\in M(I_i\times J_j).\] Its projection equals \(\bigcup_{i,j}M(I_i\times J_j)\), contains the bilinear graph, and is contained in either corresponding one-factor partitioned relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition both factor domains into a grid, select one cell, and use its local McCormick envelope. This dominates either matching one-factor partition.
assumptions_latex: \(\{I_i\}_{i=1}^P\) and \(\{J_j\}_{j=1}^Q\) are interval partitions.
\(w\) represents \(xy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_{i,j}M(I_i\times J_j)\) is a valid refinement contained in each associated one-factor relaxation.

notation.meaning: cell of the Cartesian partition grid

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Grid Error Bound and Uniform Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp product-error bound for a Cartesian grid of factor intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For interval partitions \(\{I_i\}_{i=1}^P\) and \(\{J_j\}_{j=1}^Q\), let \(R=\bigcup_{i,j}M(I_i\times J_j)\). Then \[\sup_{(x,y,w)\in R}|w-xy|=\frac14\max_{i,j}\operatorname{width}(I_i)\operatorname{width}(J_j).\] Nested refinement of either partition can only shrink \(R\). Consequently, the grid relaxations converge uniformly to the bilinear graph whenever the maximum cell width-product tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sharp grid error is one quarter of the largest cell width-product; refinement is monotone and vanishing cell errors imply uniform convergence.
assumptions_latex: Both factor domains are bounded.
The cells are the Cartesian product of two exhaustive interval partitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_R|w-xy|=\frac14\max_{i,j}\operatorname{width}(I_i)\operatorname{width}(J_j)\to0\text{ when the maximum cell width-product tends to zero.}
knowledge_statements.title: Grid Error Bound and Uniform Convergence
Adaptive Domain Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative refinement of product domains using relaxation violations or bound impact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize finite interval partitions \(\mathcal P_x,\mathcal P_y\) and construct the corresponding partitioned McCormick relaxation. At iteration \(t\), solve the relaxation and obtain \((x^t,y^t,w^t)\). If \(|w^t-x^ty^t|\leq\varepsilon\), stop. Otherwise select an active cell \(I^t\times J^t\) containing \((x^t,y^t)\), prioritizing either maximal product \((\operatorname{width} I^t)(\operatorname{width} J^t)\) or maximal observed violation, bisect both \(I^t\) and \(J^t\) at their midpoints, rebuild the affected local envelopes, and repeat. The procedure may also stop upon a valid certified optimization-gap test or a prescribed refinement limit. Every iteration produces a valid refinement. Along any nested active-cell lineage refined indefinitely by these midpoint bisections, the local McCormick product-error bound tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the relaxation, select a high-error active cell, bisect both of its factor intervals at their midpoints, and update the local envelopes. Every refinement remains valid, and the local product-error bound vanishes along any nested cell lineage refined indefinitely.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
Both intervals of every selected cell are bisected at their midpoints.
Each relaxation is solved to the accuracy required by the stopping test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iteration yields a refined valid relaxation, and along every indefinitely refined nested active-cell lineage, \((\operatorname{width} I^t)(\operatorname{width} J^t)/4\to0\).

notation.meaning: current interval partitions of the factor domains
active partition cell selected at iteration t

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Refinement Does Not Imply Global Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fairness boundary for adaptive refinement policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Refining only selected cells does not imply \(\max_{I\times J\in\mathcal C_t}\operatorname{width}(I)\operatorname{width}(J)\to0\). If a nondegenerate cell \(I\times J\) is never refined, its local McCormick hull continues to admit product error \(\operatorname{width}(I)\operatorname{width}(J)/4>0\). Thus lineage-wise convergence does not imply uniform convergence over the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence along refined lineages can coexist with a permanently coarse cell; uniform convergence requires a global mesh or fairness condition.
assumptions_latex: At least one nondegenerate partition cell is never refined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{(x,y,w)\in R_t}|w-xy|\not\to0\text{ is possible despite convergence along every indefinitely refined lineage.}

notation.meaning: union of local McCormick hulls at iteration t

knowledge_statements.title: Local Refinement Does Not Imply Global Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Convergence Under Vanishing Cell Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform convergence of nested partitioned McCormick relaxations under a vanishing maximum cell-error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_t=\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal C_t}M(C)\), where \(\mathcal C_{t+1}\) refines the finite rectangular partition \(\mathcal C_t\). Then \(R_{t+1}\subseteq R_t\), and every \((x,y,w)\in R_t\) satisfies \[|w-xy|\leq\max_{I\times J\in\mathcal C_t}\frac{\operatorname{width}(I)\operatorname{width}(J)}4.\] Consequently, if this maximum tends to zero, the relaxations converge uniformly to the graph \(w=xy\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested refinement never weakens the relaxation, and a vanishing largest cell width-product forces uniform product consistency.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C_t\) is a finite rectangular partition of a bounded product domain.
Every cell of \(\mathcal C_{t+1}\) is contained in a cell of \(\mathcal C_t\).

notation.meaning: partitioned McCormick relaxation at iteration t

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Convergence Under Vanishing Cell Error
Factor-Grouping Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive McCormick formulations indexed by binary factor-grouping trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\), choose a full binary tree whose leaves are \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). Associate an output variable \(z_v\) with every internal node \(v\); if its children represent \(z_p\) and \(z_q\), impose the McCormick inequalities for \(z_v=z_pz_q\) using valid bounds on \(z_p,z_q\). Identify the root output with \(w\). Every such tree gives a valid extended relaxation of the monomial graph, but different trees can produce different projected relaxations because intermediate-variable bounds and envelope compositions depend on the grouping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary tree specifies how factors are multiplied recursively. Each tree gives a valid McCormick relaxation, while different groupings can yield different projected strengths.
assumptions_latex: Each \(x_i\) has finite bounds.
Every intermediate product is assigned valid finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tree-defined extended system is a valid relaxation of \(w=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\).

notation.meaning: product variable associated with tree node v
root variable representing the full monomial
