knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Reuse Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharing common intermediate products across recursively linearized monomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose several monomials contain the same factor subset \(S\). A reuse formulation introduces one variable \(z_S\) for \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) and uses that variable in every recursive product containing \(S\). A copied formulation instead introduces \(z_S^{(r)}\) separately for each occurrence. Adding \(z_S^{(r)}=z_S\) for all occurrences makes the copied and reused extended formulations projection-equivalent. Without these equalities, the copied formulation may admit mutually inconsistent values for the common subproduct, so its projection contains the projection of the reuse formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One auxiliary may represent a common subproduct in every term. Independent copies are weaker unless equalities force all copies to agree.
assumptions_latex: All occurrences use the same factor subset \(S\).
The shared and copied subproducts use identical valid bounds and envelope constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\mathrm{reuse}}\subseteq R_{\mathrm{copies}}\), with equality after imposing \(z_S^{(r)}=z_S\) for every occurrence.

notation.meaning: shared auxiliary for the product over factor set S
occurrence-specific copy of the same subproduct

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Linearization Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-size formulation count for a binary recursive linearization of one monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A full binary grouping tree for the \(n\)-factor monomial \(w=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) has exactly \(n-1\) internal nodes. Consequently, recursive McCormick linearization uses \(n-1\) bilinear envelope blocks and introduces \(n-2\) intermediate product variables in addition to the designated output \(w\). If every bilinear block is represented by four inequalities, the formulation has exactly \(4(n-1)\) written envelope inequalities. Thus its extended-formulation size is \(O(n)\), excluding constraints used solely for bound computation or repeated-subexpression coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any full-binary recursive linearization of an n-factor monomial uses n−1 bilinear blocks and n−2 intermediate product variables beyond the output. Under the four-inequality convention for every block, it has exactly 4(n−1) written envelope inequalities.
assumptions_latex: The grouping structure is a full binary tree.
Each bilinear envelope block is written with four inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursive formulation uses \(n-1\) envelope blocks, \(n-2\) intermediate variables beyond \(w\), and exactly \(4(n-1)\) written envelope inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypercube Monomial Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact compact convex hull of a multilinear monomial over the unit hypercube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq2\), define \(G=\{(x,w):x\in[0,1]^n,\ w=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\}\). Its convex hull is \[\operatorname{conv}(G)=\left\{(x,w):0\leq x_i\leq1,\quad w\geq0,\quad w\leq x_i\ \text{for all }i,\quad w\geq\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-(n-1)\right\}.\] This is also the convex hull of the lifted Boolean vertices \((v,\prod_i v_i)\) with \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over the unit hypercube, the monomial hull is described by nonnegativity, one upper bound per factor, and one summed lower bound.

notation.meaning: a Boolean vertex of the hypercube

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: multilinear interpolation reduces the graph hull to lifted hypercube vertices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed unit-hypercube monomial hull is mathematically standard and the representation kind is appropriate, but no inspectable citation is supplied for the exact hull theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Box Monomial Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact vertex-based extended formulation for a multilinear monomial on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), let \(V=\prod_{i=1}^n\{\ell_i,u_i\}\), and set \(m(v)=\prod_{i=1}^n v_i\). Then the convex hull of the monomial graph over \(B\) is the projection of \[\lambda_v\geq0,\qquad \sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1,\qquad x=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vv,\qquad w=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vm(v).\] The representation is exact and uses \(2^n\) vertex weights before removal of redundant or affinely dependent columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The general-box monomial hull is the convex hull of its lifted box vertices and has an exact formulation using one convex-combination weight per vertex.
assumptions_latex: Each interval \([\ell_i,u_i]\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection of the \(\lambda\)-system equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,w):x\in B,\ w=\prod_i x_i\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a multilinear graph point is a convex combination of lifted box vertices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted-vertex convex-combination formulation is mathematically correct for a multilinear monomial over a finite box, but the exactness claim has no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Grouping Invariance on Zero-Anchored Orthant Boxes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A box class on which recursive McCormick strength does not depend on the grouping tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n I_i\), where for each \(i\), either \(I_i=[0,u_i]\) or \(I_i=[-u_i,0]\) with \(u_i>0\). For every full binary grouping tree \(T\), impose a McCormick envelope at each internal product using the exact interval bounds of that subproduct. After projection to \((x,w)\), every resulting relaxation \(R_T\) equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,w):x\in B,\ w=\prod_i x_i\}\). Hence grouping-dependent strength requires boxes outside this zero-anchored orthant class or nonexact intermediate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every factor interval has zero as an endpoint and exact subproduct bounds are used, every recursive grouping projects to the exact monomial hull; grouping differences require more general bounds or inexact propagated bounds.
assumptions_latex: For each \(i\), \(I_i=[0,u_i]\) or \(I_i=[-u_i,0]\) with \(u_i>0\).
Every internal product uses its exact finite interval bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_T=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,w):x\in B,\ w=\prod_i x_i\}\quad\text{for every full binary tree }T.

notation.meaning: projected recursive McCormick relaxation for tree T

knowledge_statements.title: Grouping Invariance on Zero-Anchored Orthant Boxes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directly checkable separation between two recursive McCormick groupings on one bounded box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(B=[1,2]^3\), compare \(T_{12}=(x_1x_2)x_3\) and \(T_{23}=x_1(x_2x_3)\). The intermediate pair products have exact bounds \([1,4]\). The point \((x_1,x_2,x_3,w)=(5/4,3/2,7/4,5/2)\) is feasible for \(T_{12}\) with \(y_{12}=7/4\). For \(T_{23}\), the McCormick inequalities imply \(y_{23}\ge5/2\) and \(w\ge y_{23}+1/4\ge11/4\), excluding that point. Conversely, \((7/4,3/2,5/4,5/2)\) is feasible for \(T_{23}\) with \(y_{23}=7/4\), while \(T_{12}\) implies \(w\ge11/4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two ternary recursive McCormick groupings are incomparable on the same positive box, as witnessed by two symmetric fractional points.
assumptions_latex: Each internal bilinear relation uses its McCormick envelope with exact bounds on its two factors; in particular, \(1\le y_{12},y_{23}\le4\).

notation.meaning: original-variable projection of the recursive McCormick relaxation for grouping tree T

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Incomparability of Ternary Groupings
Grouping-Dependent Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of recursive McCormick strength on the chosen factor grouping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded multilinear monomial, let \(R_T\) denote the projection of the recursive McCormick formulation associated with binary grouping tree \(T\). Every \(R_T\) contains the monomial graph, but for general boxes the sets \(R_T\) need not coincide. Their differences arise because each tree creates different intermediate products and therefore different propagated bounds and envelope constraints. Consequently, choosing a grouping is a relaxation-strength decision, not merely an algebraic reordering; without additional sign or bound assumptions, no fixed grouping tree universally dominates all other trees over every box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive groupings are all valid but can yield different relaxations because they create different intermediate products and bounds; no grouping is universally strongest on every box.
assumptions_latex: All original and intermediate factors have valid finite bounds.
Each internal product is relaxed by its McCormick envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For general boxes, there can exist trees \(T_1,T_2\) with \(R_{T_1}\neq R_{T_2}\), and no tree is universally dominant.

notation.meaning: projected recursive McCormick relaxation induced by T

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Grouping-dependent strength is appropriate for this container, but the universal nondominance assertion is a substantive comparative claim requiring an authoritative source or documented counterexamples.

knowledge_statements.title: Termwise-Hull Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete gap between separate term hulls and the joint graph hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([0,1]^3\), consider \(w_{12}=x_1x_2\), \(w_{13}=x_1x_3\), and \(w_{23}=x_2x_3\). The point \[x_1=x_2=x_3=\tfrac12,\qquad w_{12}=w_{13}=\tfrac12,\qquad w_{23}=0\] belongs to the intersection of the three individual bilinear graph hulls. It does not belong to the convex hull of the joint graph: at Boolean vertices, \(w_{12}=w_{13}=1\) forces \(x_1=x_2=x_3=1\), which also forces \(w_{23}=1\); convex averaging preserves the resulting incompatibility. Hence separate termwise hulls can be strictly weaker than the joint hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three pairwise product hulls admit a fractional point whose product values cannot arise jointly, proving that separate exact term hulls need not give the joint hull.
assumptions_latex: Each pairwise product is convexified separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{ij}\operatorname{conv}\{(x,w_{ij}):w_{ij}=x_ix_j\}\) strictly contains the convex hull of the joint three-product graph.

notation.meaning: lifted variable representing pairwise product x_i x_j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated fractional point does satisfy the three separate McCormick hulls and is incompatible with the joint hull, but no source is supplied. The Boolean-vertex and convex-averaging explanation is also proof-like text and should be removed when a sourced candidate is prepared.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit recursive-relaxation point removed by equating two copies of a common subproduct.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([0,1]^4\), recursively formulate \(w_1=(x_1x_2)x_3\) and \(w_2=(x_1x_2)x_4\) using separate auxiliaries \(y_1,y_2\) for \(x_1x_2\). The point \[x_1=x_2=\tfrac12,\quad x_3=x_4=1,\quad y_1=w_1=\tfrac12,\quad y_2=w_2=0\] satisfies every McCormick block in the copied formulation. It violates the consistency equation \(y_1=y_2\), and its projected values violate \(w_1=w_2\), which is valid when \(x_3=x_4=1\). Thus sharing or equating the common-subproduct auxiliaries can strictly strengthen the projected relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two copied relaxations can assign different values to the same common product. A specified unit-box point is feasible with separate copies but is removed by sharing or equating them.
assumptions_latex: Each bilinear node uses its unit-box McCormick envelope.
The two auxiliaries represent the same subproduct \(x_1x_2\).

notation.meaning: occurrence-specific auxiliary for x_1x_2 in term r

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Strengthening from Shared-Subproduct Consistency
Overlapping-Factor Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency constraints for repeated subproducts shared by overlapping multilinear terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let recursive formulations for terms indexed by \(r\in\mathcal R\) contain auxiliaries \(z_S^{(r)}\) intended to represent the same subproduct \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\). Overlapping-factor consistency requires \[z_S^{(r)}=z_S^{(s)}\qquad\text{for every }r,s\in\mathcal R\text{ containing the represented occurrence of }S.\] Equivalently, introduce one shared variable \(z_S\) and substitute it for every copy. These equalities are valid for the joint nonlinear graph and can strictly strengthen the intersection of independently constructed term relaxations by excluding incompatible values assigned to a common subproduct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliaries representing the same overlapping subproduct must agree. Sharing one variable, or equating all copies, removes inconsistent combinations allowed by independent term relaxations.
assumptions_latex: Each \(z_S^{(r)}\) is intended to represent exactly \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\).
All occurrences refer to the same original factor variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joint consistency is enforced by \(z_S^{(r)}=z_S^{(s)}\) for all relevant occurrences, or by replacing them with one \(z_S\).

notation.meaning: index set of a common factor subset
term-r auxiliary for the product over S
set of terms containing the common subproduct

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Equality or sharing of auxiliaries for the same subproduct is a valid consistency condition. However, the claim that these constraints can strictly strengthen independently constructed relaxations requires an inspectable source or documented example.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a bounded scalar \(x\in[\ell,u]\), introduce \(w\) for \(x^2\). The convex hull of the graph of the square over the interval is
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{(x,x^2):x\in[\ell,u]\}
=
\{(x,w):\ell\le x\le u,\ x^2\le w,\ w\le(\ell+u)x-\ell u\}.
\]
Thus the convex quadratic epigraph inequality and the secant upper bound give the exact convex relaxation in the lifted \((x,w)\)-space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded square is relaxed exactly by placing its lifted value above the parabola and below the interval secant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Tangent Approximation of the Square Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear outer approximation of the nonlinear epigraph side and its exact uniform error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq[\ell,u]\) be nonempty and finite. Replacing \(w\geq x^2\) by \[w\geq2tx-t^2\qquad(t\in T)\] and retaining \(w\leq(\ell+u)x-\ell u\) gives a polyhedral outer relaxation of the square-graph hull. Its lower-envelope error is \[x^2-\max_{t\in T}(2tx-t^2)=\min_{t\in T}(x-t)^2.\] Hence the uniform lower error is the squared covering radius of \(T\) on \([\ell,u]\) and tends to zero when that radius vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parabola tangents plus the secant give an LP outer approximation whose exact lower error is the squared distance to the nearest tangent point.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a nonempty finite subset of \([\ell,u]\).
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Tangent Approximation of the Square Hull

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Secant Gap for a Bounded Square
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum vertical gap in the exact lifted convex hull of a scalar square.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in[\ell,u]\), the gap between the secant \(s(x)=(\ell+u)x-\ell u\) and the parabola is \[s(x)-x^2=(x-\ell)(u-x).\] Its maximum is \((u-\ell)^2/4\), attained at \(x=(\ell+u)/2\); the gap vanishes identically when \(\ell=u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square-hull gap is the product of the distances to the endpoints and reaches one quarter of the squared interval width at the midpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\leq u\) are finite.

notation.meaning: secant of the square through the interval endpoints

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\in\mathbb N\) be positive, let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(\ell_i\le x_i\le u_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), and consider constraints \(x^{\mathsf T}Q^k x+(c^k)^{\mathsf T}x\le b_k\) for \(k=1,\ldots,m\), where \(Q^k\in\mathbb S^n\), \(c^k\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b_k\in\mathbb R\). Introduce symmetric variables \(W_{ij}=W_{ji}\) representing \(x_i x_j\), and replace each quadratic form by \(\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n Q^k_{ij}W_{ij}\). For \(1\le i<j\le n\), impose the four McCormick inequalities over \([\ell_i,u_i]\times[\ell_j,u_j]\); for \(i=j\), impose \(x_i^2\le W_{ii}\le(\ell_i+u_i)x_i-\ell_i u_i\). Every feasible point of the original bounded QCQP system has the lifted extension \(W=xx^{\mathsf T}\), so the resulting system is a valid convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each quadratic monomial in a bounded finite-dimensional QCQP is lifted separately and constrained by its square or bilinear convex-hull inequalities, yielding a valid convex relaxation of all quadratic constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{\{i,j\}:i<j,\ Q^k_{ij}\neq0\text{ for some }k\}\) and \(D=\{i:Q^k_{ii}\neq0\text{ for some }k\}\). A sparse termwise construction uses \(|E|+|D|\) lifted variables, four McCormick inequalities per pair in \(E\), and one square-epigraph plus one secant inequality per index in \(D\), in addition to the \(m\) lifted quadratic constraints. Its written envelope size is \(4|E|+2|D|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting unused products makes formulation size linear in the union of quadratic supports: four envelope inequalities per bilinear term and two per square.
assumptions_latex: Only monomials with a nonzero coefficient in at least one retained quadratic expression are lifted.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-bound requirement and joint-consistency limitation of independent termwise envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finite McCormick inequalities for \(W_{ij}=x_ix_j\) require finite lower and upper bounds for both factors; if a required bound is infinite, the standard finite envelope cannot be formed. Even with finite bounds, imposing each product hull separately guarantees only termwise consistency and does not generally impose the joint identity \(W=xx^{\mathsf T}\). The lifted relaxation may therefore contain matrices that do not arise from any common vector \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard envelopes require finite factor bounds, and separately valid product hulls do not enforce a common rank-one lifted matrix.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation uses independent square and bilinear hull constraints without the rank-one equation or sufficient additional coupling constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Termwise envelope feasibility}\not\Longrightarrow W=xx^{\mathsf T}\text{ in general.}

notation.meaning: matrix of separately lifted quadratic products

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be bounded, let \(q_k:D\to\mathbb R\) for \(k=1,\ldots,m\), and suppose the original feasible set is \(F=\{x\in D:q_k(x)\le0\text{ for }k=1,\ldots,m\}\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), define \(q_\lambda(x)=\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_kq_k(x)\). Every \(x\in F\) satisfies \(q_\lambda(x)\le0\). If \(g_\lambda:D\to\mathbb R\) is convex and satisfies \(g_\lambda(x)\le q_\lambda(x)\) for every \(x\in D\), then \[g_\lambda(x)\le0\] is a valid convex relaxation of \(F\). Convexifying the aggregate can preserve interactions among terms that termwise relaxations may omit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraints may be combined with nonnegative weights and then convexly underestimated; the resulting convex inequality is valid for every point feasible for the original constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed Aggregation Need Not Be Valid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign boundary for aggregating inequalities with a common less-than-or-equal orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(q_k(x)\leq0\), arbitrary signed aggregation is not generally valid. On \(D=[-1,1]\), the inequality \(q_1(x)=x\leq0\) does not imply the negatively weighted aggregate \(-q_1(x)=-x\leq0\), because the feasible point \(x=-1\) violates the aggregate. Thus negative weights require additional problem-specific justification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative multiplier can reverse an inequality and cut off feasible points; nonnegative weights are the general validity condition absent additional structure.
assumptions_latex: Original inequalities have the orientation \(q_k(x)\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda\notin\mathbb R_+^m\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_k\lambda_kq_k(x)\leq0\text{ need not be valid on the original feasible set.}
knowledge_statements.title: Signed Aggregation Need Not Be Valid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance and normalization of the family obtained by convexifying every nonnegative aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty compact convex set, let each \(q_k:D\to\mathbb R\) be finite, and for \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) define \(q_\lambda=\sum_k\lambda_kq_k\). If \(\operatorname{vex}_Dq_\lambda\) denotes the convex envelope on \(D\), set \[R_{\mathrm{agg}}=\{x\in D:(\operatorname{vex}_Dq_\lambda)(x)\leq0\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\}.\] Since every unit vector \(e_k\) is admissible, \[R_{\mathrm{agg}}\subseteq\{x\in D:(\operatorname{vex}_Dq_k)(x)\leq0\ \forall k\}.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{vex}_D(q_{\alpha\lambda})=\alpha\operatorname{vex}_D(q_\lambda)\) for \(\alpha>0\), so nonzero weights may be normalized, for example by \(\sum_k\lambda_k=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family of all nonnegative convexified aggregates includes the individual convexifications and may be normalized because positive rescaling is redundant.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Each \(q_k\) is finite on \(D\).
Aggregation weights are nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(i\ne j\), \(x_i\in[\ell_i,u_i]\), and \(x_j\in[\ell_j,u_j]\), where both intervals have finite endpoints. The four products \[(x_i-\ell_i)(x_j-\ell_j),\quad (x_i-\ell_i)(u_j-x_j),\quad (u_i-x_i)(x_j-\ell_j),\quad (u_i-x_i)(u_j-x_j)\] are nonnegative. Expanding them and replacing \(x_i x_j\) by \(W_{ij}\) yields exactly the four McCormick inequalities. Every point satisfying \(W_{ij}=x_i x_j\) satisfies these inequalities, and their system describes the convex hull of the bilinear graph over \([\ell_i,u_i]\times[\ell_j,u_j]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two distinct bounded variables, multiplying pairs of nonnegative lower- and upper-bound factors and relinearizing produces the four McCormick inequalities and the bilinear graph's convex hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(g(x)\ge0\) is valid on the original feasible set and \(h(x)\ge0\) throughout its bounded domain; typical choices are \(h(x)=x_i-\ell_i\) and \(h(x)=u_i-x_i\). Then every feasible point satisfies \(g(x)h(x)\ge0\). Expand this product and apply the monomial substitution map \(\mathcal R(x^\alpha)=y_\alpha\). The resulting lifted linear inequality
\[
\mathcal R\bigl(g(x)h(x)\bigr)\ge0
\]
is valid whenever the lifted variables take their exact monomial values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid constraint multiplied by any certified nonnegative bound or constraint factor remains valid and becomes linear after monomial lifting.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\) be positive and let \(M\subset\mathbb N^n\) be finite, contain \(0\), and contain the unit exponents required for the original variables. The RLT relinearization space is \(\mathbb R^M\), with one coordinate \(y_\alpha\) for each \(\alpha\in M\), intended to represent \(x^\alpha\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An RLT relinearization space has one coordinate for every selected monomial, and its linear substitution operator maps each supported polynomial into those lifted coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic and realizability limits of the monomial-substitution operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(\mathcal R_M\) is linear on polynomials supported in \(M\), but it is not an algebra homomorphism into the free lifted-coordinate space. Even when \(p\), \(q\), and \(pq\) are supported, in general \[\mathcal R_M(pq)\ne \mathcal R_M(p)\mathcal R_M(q).\] Moreover, an arbitrary \(y\in\mathbb R^M\) need not equal \((x^\alpha)_{\alpha\in M}\) for any \(x\). Exact monomial realizability therefore requires consistency relations beyond membership in the free coordinate space; an RLT relaxation imposes only its selected linear consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relinearization is a linear substitution, not multiplication and not by itself a certificate that lifted coordinates are genuine monomial values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a base relaxation, a finite candidate pool \(P\) of valid relinearized product inequalities, a row budget \(B\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\). Solve the current relaxation at \(z^*\), compute each candidate violation \(v_p\), and select at most \(B\) candidates with \(v_p>\varepsilon\), using a prescribed score such as normalized violation. Output the final relaxation and its bound; validity follows because every added row belongs to \(P\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery and stopping conditions for selection from a finite RLT row pool.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite pool of valid RLT inequalities for a fixed linear objective. Suppose each current relaxation is solved exactly, separation examines every row in \(P\), at least one previously unadded row violated by more than \(\varepsilon=0\) is added whenever one exists, and added rows are never removed. Then there are at most \(|P|\) successful addition rounds. When no row in \(P\) is violated at the current optimum, that optimum is feasible and optimal for the relaxation containing the full pool \(P\). With \(\varepsilon>0\) or incomplete separation, stopping certifies only tolerance satisfaction or satisfaction of the searched subpool, not exact full-pool optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaustive exact separation over a finite retained pool recovers the full-pool optimum after finitely many additions; tolerances or incomplete searches weaken the certificate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes operational stopping from a certificate that the entire declared RLT family is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stopping because a per-round cut limit, iteration limit, time limit, numerical filter, or restricted pricing search is reached does not certify that every admissible RLT inequality is satisfied. A no-violated-row result is valid only relative to the family actually and soundly searched. It certifies \(\varepsilon\)-satisfaction of the full declared family only when separation over that family is exhaustive and numerically reliable at tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operational cut-loop termination is not a full-RLT separation certificate unless the declared family was searched exhaustively and soundly.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incomplete Terminal Family Need Not Be Exact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of terminal exactness after omitting a required literal product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in[0,1]:x\le\tfrac12\}\). Its binary feasible-set hull is \(\{0\}\). At the terminal one-variable level, multiplying \(\tfrac12-x\ge0\) by \(x\) and using \(x^2=x\) yields \(-\tfrac12x\ge0\), which enforces \(x=0\). If this product row is omitted, the retained original relaxation still contains \(x=\tfrac12\), so the nominal terminal but incomplete family is not the binary hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even at the nominal terminal level, omitting a required product row can prevent recovery of the binary hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nesting and Terminal Exactness of Complete Binary RLT
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected strength of the complete binary literal-product hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in[0,1]^n:Ax\le b\}\). For \(0\le d\le n\), form the complete level-\(d\) binary RLT system by multiplying every defining inequality, including the bound inequalities, by every product of at most \(d\) literals on distinct indices, multilinearizing with \(x_i^2=x_i\), and identifying equal squarefree monomials. Let \(Q_d\) be its projection onto the original \(x\)-space. Then \[\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\{0,1\}^n)\subseteq Q_{d+1}\subseteq Q_d\quad(0\le d<n),\] and the terminal level is exact: \[Q_n=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\{0,1\}^n).\] The exactness guarantee depends on using the complete declared product family and consistent monomial identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete binary RLT levels are nested and terminate at the binary integer hull.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq[0,1]^n\) is described by linear inequalities together with its bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested strength of the binary RLT hierarchy under a fixed literal-product convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in[0,1]^n:Ax\le b\}\) and let \(R_d(P)\) be the level-\(d\) RLT relaxation obtained by multiplying every defining inequality by all nonnegative products of at most \(d\) literals from \(\{x_j,1-x_j\}_{j=1}^n\), expanding, and consistently linearizing monomials. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Combinatorial Size of a Full Binary RLT Level
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row and auxiliary-variable counts under an explicit full literal-multiplier convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(m\) defining inequalities in \(n\) binary variables. At level \(d\), use every product of at most \(d\) literals on distinct indices, choosing independently either \(x_i\) or \(1-x_i\) on each selected index, and globally share squarefree monomial coordinates. Before removing duplicate or identically zero generated rows, the number of inequality instances is \[m\sum_{j=0}^{\min\{d,n\}}2^j\binom nj.\] If original variables are not counted as auxiliaries, at most \[\sum_{k=2}^{\min\{d+1,n\}}\binom nk\] nontrivial monomial variables are needed. Hence these combinatorial counts are polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \(d\), while the full range \(d=n\) has \(m3^n\) raw row instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a declared full literal-product convention, fixed RLT levels have polynomial combinatorial size, while unrestricted levels can have exponentially many generated rows.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) binary variables and \(m\) defining inequality rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Size of a Full Binary RLT Level
Level-Dependent Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial formulation growth for a literal-product binary RLT construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(P\) has \(n\) binary variables and \(m\) defining inequalities. At level \(d\), there are at most \[m\sum_{j=0}^{d}2^j\binom{n}{j}\] generated inequality instances before removing repetitions and contradictions. After literal products are expanded and identical monomials are shared, at most \[\sum_{k=2}^{d+1}\binom{n}{k}\] nontrivial monomial variables are needed. Thus fixed-level size is polynomial in \(n\), whereas levels growing with \(n\) may have exponential size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level d has polynomial size for fixed d, but its literal products and monomial variables grow combinatorially and may become exponential.
assumptions_latex: Each multiplier uses distinct variable indices and at most \(d\) literals.
Square-free binary monomials are shared globally.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-M On-Off Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row-wise big-M representation of a bounded indicator implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and consider the implication \(z=1\Rightarrow Ax\le b\). For every row \(i\), choose a finite constant satisfying \[M_i\ge\sup_{x\in X}(a_i^\top x-b_i).\] Then the implication is represented over integer \(z\) by \[x\in X,\qquad a_i^\top x\le b_i+M_i(1-z)\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] The smallest valid row constant is the displayed supremum; larger constants preserve integer validity but can weaken the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid row-wise M deactivates each inequality when z is zero; minimal valid constants give the strongest formulation of this form.
assumptions_latex: \(M_i<+\infty\) for every row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The big-M inequalities are equivalent over \(X\times\{0,1\}\) to \(z=1\Rightarrow Ax\le b\).

notation.meaning: valid deactivation constant for row i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Big-M Representation of an Activated Equality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided row-wise big-M encoding of an equality guarded by binary activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb R^n, z\in\{0,1\}, and consider z=1\Rightarrow a^\top x=b. Choose finite nonnegative constants M^+\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-b) and M^-\geq\sup_{x\in X}(b-a^\top x). Then the implication is represented exactly over X\times\{0,1\} by a^\top x-b\leq M^+(1-z) and b-a^\top x\leq M^-(1-z). Under the nonnegative-big-M convention, the tightest constants are the corresponding suprema truncated below at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An activated equality uses separate upper- and lower-deviation big-M rows, each bounded over the inactive domain.
assumptions_latex: \sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-b)<+\infty.
\sup_{x\in X}(b-a^\top x)<+\infty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(x,z)\in X\times\{0,1\}:z=1\Rightarrow a^\top x=b\}=\{(x,z)\in X\times\{0,1\}:a^\top x-b\leq M^+(1-z),\ b-a^\top x\leq M^-(1-z)\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variable-copy formulation for a two-state polyhedral union, including its unbounded endpoint condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_k=\{x:A^kx\le b^k\}\) be nonempty polyhedra with \(\operatorname{rec}(P_0)=\operatorname{rec}(P_1)\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}((P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\}))\) is the projection of \[x=x^0+x^1,\quad A^0x^0\le b^0(1-z),\quad A^1x^1\le b^1z,\quad 0\le z\le1.\] Bounded disjuncts satisfy the condition because both recession cones are \(\{0\}\). Without recession compatibility the formulation can be inexact even for binary \(z\): for \(P_0=\{0\}\) and \(P_1=[0,\infty)\), its \(z=0\) slice admits every \(x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disaggregated scaled copies give the two-disjunct convex hull when the disjuncts have a common recession cone; otherwise an unselected copy can introduce spurious recession directions.
assumptions_latex: \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) are nonempty polyhedra.
\(\operatorname{rec}(P_0)=\operatorname{rec}(P_1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed extended formulation projects to \(\operatorname{conv}((P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\}))\).

notation.meaning: homogenized variable copy for state k

Disaggregated On-Off Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balas-style disaggregation for a bounded two-term on-off union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_k=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:A^ku\le b^k\}\) be nonempty bounded polyhedra for \(k\in\{0,1\}\). The convex hull of \[(P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\})\] is the projection of \[x=x^0+x^1,\qquad A^0x^0\le b^0(1-z),\qquad A^1x^1\le b^1z,\qquad 0\le z\le1.\] For the off state \(P_0=\{0\}\), this reduces to a scaled on-state copy with \(x=x^1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate variable copies for the off and on states produce an extended formulation of the convex hull of the two-state union.
assumptions_latex: \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) are nonempty bounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projecting the displayed system onto \((x,z)\) yields \(\operatorname{conv}((P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\}))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Native Indicator Semantics and Relaxation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent binary semantics and solver-dependent continuous treatment of native on-off implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(0\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(z\in\{0,1\}\). The native implications \[z=1\Rightarrow Ax\le b,\qquad z=0\Rightarrow x=0,\qquad x\in X\] have feasible set \[\bigl(\{0\}\times\{0\}\bigr)\cup\bigl((X\cap\{x:Ax\le b\})\times\{1\}\bigr).\] The logical object alone does not define a continuous relaxation for fractional \(z\); that relaxation is determined by the implementation or reformulation selected by the solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paired native implications exactly define the binary on-off union, but native syntax by itself specifies no unique fractional relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The modeling interface implements the displayed implications with their stated logical semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary feasible set is the displayed union, while no solver-independent fractional relaxation follows from the native syntax alone.

notation.meaning: ambient domain of the continuous variables

knowledge_statements.title: Native Indicator Semantics and Relaxation Boundary
Indicator-Native Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical on-off constraints retained natively rather than expanded with explicit constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the indicator-native system \[z=1\Rightarrow Ax\le b,\qquad z=0\Rightarrow x=0\] represents the union \[\bigl(\{0\}\times\{0\}\bigr)\cup\bigl((X\cap\{x:Ax\le b\})\times\{1\}\bigr).\] This is a logical mixed-integer representation: its integer feasible set is solver-independent, but its node relaxation is not determined until a solver supplies bounds, cuts, branching, or an internal reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Native indicator constraints describe the on-off union exactly at binary solutions without exposing big-M constants, but do not uniquely specify an LP relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The modeling system supports indicator implications.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer feasible set equals the displayed two-term union.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact component lifting for an additively separable cost activated by one common indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\), where each \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex. For one common scaling variable \(z\ge0\), \[\bar p_f(x,z)=\sum_{i=1}^n\bar p_{f_i}(x_i,z).\] Hence its epigraph is represented by \[t\ge\sum_i t_i,\qquad t_i\ge\bar p_{f_i}(x_i,z)\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] The same \(z\) must occur in every component; independent fractional activations represent a different disjunction unless constraints identify them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additively separable cost may be perspectivized componentwise when every component uses the same common activation variable.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex.
One common activation variable scales all components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar p_{\sum_i f_i}(x,z)=\sum_i\bar p_{f_i}(x_i,z)\), and the displayed epigraph lifting is exact.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-perspective convex hull for one bounded scalar term with its own indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, and assume \([\ell,u]\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\) with finite \(\ell\le u\). The closed convex hull of \[\{(0,0,t):t\ge0\}\cup\{(x,1,t):\ell\le x\le u,\ t\ge f(x)\}\] is \[0\le z\le1,\quad \ell z\le x\le uz,\quad t\ge\bar p_f(x,z),\] where \(\bar p_f(x,z)=zf(x/z)\) for \(z>0\) and \(\bar p_f(x,0)=f^\infty(x)\). The scaled bounds force \(x=0\) at \(z=0\), so no assumption \(f(0)=0\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded scalar on-off epigraph is convexified by scaled bounds and the closed perspective; normalization at the active function's origin is unnecessary.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\ell\) and \(u\) are finite with \(\ell\le u\).
\([\ell,u]\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed closed-perspective system is the closed convex hull of the scalar on-off epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Scalar On-Off Epigraph Hull
Separable Convex On-Off Terms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective convexification of separable scalar on-off epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\), let \(f_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be closed proper convex with \(f_i(0)=0\), and impose \(\ell_i z_i\le x_i\le u_i z_i\), where \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\ell_i,u_i\) are finite. The closed convex hull of \[z_i\in\{0,1\},\quad z_i=0\Rightarrow x_i=0,\quad t_i\ge f_i(x_i)\] is described by \[0\le z_i\le1,\quad \ell_i z_i\le x_i\le u_i z_i,\quad t_i\ge\widetilde f_i(x_i,z_i),\] where \(\widetilde f_i(x_i,z_i)=z_i f_i(x_i/z_i)\) for \(z_i>0\) and is closed at \(z_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each bounded separable convex on-off epigraph is convexified by replacing its function with the closed perspective and relaxing the indicator to [0,1].
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is closed, proper, convex, and satisfies \(f_i(0)=0\).
The bounds \(\ell_i,u_i\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed-perspective system gives the convex hull of each scalar on-off epigraph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar and vector rotated-cone formulation, including the singular zero-slice boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\), let \(Q=R^\top R\), and set \(f(x)=x^\top Qx+c^\top x+d\). Its closed-perspective epigraph is \[z\ge0,\quad a=t-c^\top x-dz\ge0,\quad \|Rx\|_2^2\le za.\] Equivalently, \((a,z,\sqrt2Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r\), where \(\mathcal Q_r=\{(u,v,w):u,v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\). For \(z>0\) this is \(t\ge x^\top Qx/z+c^\top x+dz\). At \(z=0\), it permits exactly \(x\in\ker Q\) with \(t\ge c^\top x\); thus \(Q\succ0\) forces \(x=0\), whereas singular \(Q\) requires additional links if every off-state component must vanish. The scalar case \(Q=q>0\) gives \(qx^2\le tz\) after omitting affine terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic perspective is one rotated-SOC constraint; singular quadratic forms retain their kernel at zero activation unless other links remove it.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\succeq0\).
\(Q=R^\top R\).
The rotated cone uses the displayed normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rotated-SOC system is exactly the closed-perspective epigraph of the affine-quadratic function.

notation.meaning: rotated second-order cone in the displayed normalization

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Quadratic Perspective
Quadratic On-Off Terms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated-cone perspective formulation for a scalar convex quadratic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q>0\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and require \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0\) with epigraph variable \(t\). The closed perspective relaxation of \(t\ge qx^2\) is \[0\le z\le1,\qquad t\ge0,
\qquad qx^2\le tz.\] Equivalently, it is the rotated second-order-cone constraint \[(t,z,\sqrt{2q}\,x)\in\mathcal Q_r^3,\qquad \mathcal Q_r^3=\{(a,b,c):a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ 2ab\ge c^2\}.\] With finite on-state bounds, adding their scaled forms completes the bounded on-off formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perspective of a nonnegative scalar quadratic is represented exactly by one rotated second-order-cone constraint linking x, t, and the activation variable.
assumptions_latex: The off state requires \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge qx^2/z\) for \(z>0\), with its closure at \(z=0\), is equivalent to \(qx^2\le tz\), \(t,z\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nonquadratic conic representation of a closed on-off perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}\), the constraint \[(x,z,t)\in K_{\exp}\] represents \(t\ge z\exp(x/z)\) for \(z>0\) and its closed-perspective boundary at \(z=0\). That boundary is \(x\le0\), \(t\ge0\); therefore a model requiring the singleton off state \(x=0\) must impose an additional activation link excluding \(x<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential cone directly represents the closed perspective of the exponential function, including its nontrivial recession boundary.
assumptions_latex: The exponential cone uses the displayed coordinate convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,z,t)\in K_{\exp}\) is equivalent to the closed-perspective epigraph of \(e^x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Cone Perspective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic Homogenization Criterion for Perspective Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact zero-slice criterion for homogenizing a lifted conic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be a nonempty closed convex epigraph with representation \(E=\{(x,t):\exists y,\ Ax+Bt+Cy+d\in K\}\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. Define \[H=\{(x,t,z):z\ge0,\ \exists y,\ Ax+Bt+Cy+dz\in K\}.\] For every \(z>0\), the \(z\)-slice of \(H\) is \(zE\). If \(H\) is closed and its zero slice projects exactly to \(\operatorname{rec}(E)\), then \[H=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(E\times\{1\}),\] the closed-perspective epigraph. Requiring the zero slice to be only \((x,t)=(0,0)\) is generally wrong for epigraphs, whose recession cone always contains nonnegative vertical directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing the affine offset yields a closed perspective exactly when the projected zero slice matches the epigraph recession cone; it should not generally be forced to a single point.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a nonempty closed convex epigraph.
\(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The homogenized projection \(H\) is closed.
The projected zero slice of \(H\) equals \(\operatorname{rec}(E)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Homogenization Criterion for Perspective Epigraphs
Conic-Representable On-Off Terms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenized conic formulation of an activated convex epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and suppose the on-state epigraph has representation \[E=\{(x,t):\exists y,\ Ax+Bt+Cy+d\in K\}.\] Its homogenized perspective formulation is \[0\le z\le1,\qquad \exists y:\ Ax+Bt+Cy+dz\in K.\] If the zero slice of this system projects only to \((x,t)=(0,0)\), then it is the closed conic hull of \(E\times\{1\}\) and hence represents the closed perspective epigraph. Scaled variable bounds may be added to enforce the required zero slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic epigraph is perspectivized by multiplying its affine offset by the activation variable, provided the zero slice contains no unwanted projected recession points.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The zero slice projects only to \((x,t)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The homogenized conic system represents the closed perspective epigraph of \(E\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct functional representation of a closed convex perspective, including zero activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed proper convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), its closed perspective is \[f^\pi(x,z)=\begin{cases}z f(x/z),&z>0,\\ f^\infty(x),&z=0,\\ +\infty,&z<0.\end{cases}\] The direct perspective representation is \(t\ge f^\pi(x,z)\), together with any perspectivized domain constraints needed to impose the intended off state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The direct representation uses the closed perspective function itself; its zero-activation value is the recession function, not an arbitrary convention.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Direct Perspective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical conjugate representation of the direct perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closed proper convex \(f\), \[f^\pi(x,z)=\sup_{y\in\operatorname{dom}f^*}\bigl\{y^\top x-zf^*(y)\bigr\},\qquad z\ge0.\] Hence its epigraph is the intersection of the halfspaces \(t\ge y^\top x-zf^*(y)\) over \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The direct perspective is the supremum of homogeneous affine supports indexed by the Fenchel conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Support Formula

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of using only z f(x/z) without its closed endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The expression \(zf(x/z)\) is defined only for \(z>0\). Assigning an arbitrary value at \(z=0\), or simply omitting that slice, can destroy lower semicontinuity or admit incorrect recession directions. The closed endpoint must be \(f^\infty(x)\), supplemented by domain constraints when the modeled off state is smaller than the recession slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-activation formula alone is not a closed direct perspective; the recession endpoint and off-state domain are essential.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties of the direct closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex, then \(f^\pi\) is closed, proper, convex, and positively homogeneous: \[f^\pi(\lambda x,\lambda z)=\lambda f^\pi(x,z)\qquad(\lambda\ge0).\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}f^\pi\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex perspective is itself closed, convex, and positively homogeneous, so its epigraph is conic.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\pi\text{ is closed, proper, convex, and positively homogeneous.}
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Homogeneous Structure
Direct Perspective Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective epigraph written directly in the original activation variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be closed proper convex with \(f(0)=0\). Define its closed perspective by \[f^\pi(x,z)=\begin{cases}z f(x/z),&z>0,\\ f^\infty(x),&z=0,\\ +\infty,&z<0,\end{cases}\] where \(f^\infty\) is the recession function. The direct perspective representation is \[0\le z\le1,
\qquad t\ge f^\pi(x,z).\] If scaled bounds force \(x=0\) at \(z=0\), this system is the closed convex hull of the corresponding on-off epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The direct formulation places the closed perspective function itself in the epigraph inequality, with scaled bounds enforcing the intended off state.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex with \(f(0)=0\).
Scaled domain constraints enforce \(x=0\) when \(z=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge f^\pi(x,z)\), together with the scaled domain, represents the closed convex hull of the on-off epigraph.
review_flags: A source for the closed-perspective endpoint and convex-hull statement is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of conic homogenization when the lifted recession slice is too large or too small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Agreement of a homogenized conic system with the positive-activation formula does not establish exactness at \(z=0\). If \[\{(x,t):\exists w,\ Ax+Bt+Cw\in K\}\ne\{(x,t):t\ge f^\infty(x)\},\] after including the intended off-state domain, the conic system is not the closed perspective epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Correct behavior for positive activation is insufficient: a mismatched homogeneous zero slice makes the conic perspective formulation inexact.
assumptions_latex: The homogenized conic system is well defined at \(z=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rotated-Cone Perspective of a Positive-Semidefinite Quadratic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical rotated-second-order-cone instance of conic perspective homogenization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=L^\top L\succeq0\) and \(\mathcal Q_r=\{(a,b,c):2ab\ge\|c\|_2^2,\ a,b\ge0\}\). Then \[z\ge0,\qquad (t/2,z,Lx)\in\mathcal Q_r\] represents the closed perspective inequality \(t\ge x^\top Qx/z\) for \(z>0\), with zero slice \(Lx=0\) and \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perspective of a positive-semidefinite quadratic has an exact rotated-second-order-cone representation, whose zero slice allows precisely the quadratic's recession directions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=L^\top L\succeq0\).
\(\mathcal Q_r\) uses the convention \(2ab\ge\|c\|_2^2\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact homogenization of a lifted conic epigraph, including its zero-activation slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(u,\tau):\exists v,\ Au+B\tau+Cv+d\in K\}\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. Its homogenization is \[H=\{(x,z,t):z\ge0,\ \exists w,\ Ax+Bt+Cw+dz\in K\}.\] For \(z>0\), \((x,z,t)\in H\) is equivalent to \(t\ge zf(x/z)\). The formulation represents the closed perspective epigraph exactly when its slice at \(z=0\) equals \(\{(x,0,t):t\ge f^\infty(x)\}\), together with any required off-state domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted conic epigraph can be homogenized to represent its perspective; exactness additionally requires the homogenized zero slice to match the recession epigraph and intended off state.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The original lifted system represents \(\operatorname{epi}f\) exactly.
The homogenized zero slice matches the required recession and off-state slice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H=\operatorname{epi}f^\pi\text{ under the stated zero-slice condition.}
knowledge_statements.title: Homogenized Conic Perspective Representation
Conic Perspective Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-preserving homogenization of a lifted convex epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\operatorname{epi}f\) admits the lifted conic description \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(u,\tau):\exists v,\ Au+B\tau+Cv+d\in K\},\] with \(K\) a closed convex cone. A conic perspective representation is \[0\le z\le1,\qquad \exists w:\ Ax+Bt+Cw+dz\in K.\] For \(z>0\), division by \(z\) recovers \(t\ge zf(x/z)\). If its zero slice matches the recession epigraph and the intended off-state constraints, the system is closed and exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing a lifted conic epigraph yields its perspective while retaining conic form, subject to a correct zero-slice or recession condition.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The homogenized zero slice equals the required recession epigraph and off state.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+2+p}\) in variables \((x,z,t,w)\) is a projected perspective representation of \(f\) when \[\operatorname{proj}_{x,z,t}F=\operatorname{epi}f^\pi.\] If only \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{proj}_{x,z,t}F)=\operatorname{epi}f^\pi\), it is a closed-projection representation and not necessarily an exact unclosed projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected perspective formulation is a lift whose existential projection is exactly the closed perspective epigraph; equality only after closure must be distinguished.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and attainment boundary for projected perspective formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed. Consequently, a closed lifted set \(F\) may satisfy \[\operatorname{proj}F\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{proj}F)=\operatorname{epi}f^\pi.\] Without attainment or another closed-image condition, equality of the closure does not justify an exact projected-perspective claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex lift can have a nonclosed projection, so attainment or another closed-projection condition is essential for exactness without closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perspective of an Attained Infimal Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Substantive projected construction obtained by perspectivizing a lifted convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb R^{n+p}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be closed proper convex and let \(f(x)=\inf_y g(x,y)\). Assume \(f\) is closed and the infima defining \(f\) and the corresponding recession value are attained. Then, for \(z\ge0\), \[f^\pi(x,z)=\inf_w g^\pi(x,w,z),\] and therefore \[t\ge f^\pi(x,z)\iff\exists w:\ t\ge g^\pi(x,w,z).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under closedness and attainment, perspectivization commutes with infimal projection and yields an exact lifted formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is closed, proper, and convex.
\(f(x)=\inf_y g(x,y)\) is closed.
The relevant primal and recession infima are attained.

notation.meaning: closed perspective of the lifted function g

Projected Perspective Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective epigraph obtained by projecting an exact lifted formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+2+p}\) be a closed convex lifted perspective set in variables \((x,z,t,y)\), and define \[S=\{(x,z,t):\exists y,\ (x,z,t,y)\in F\}.\] If \(S=\{(x,z,t):0\le z\le1,\ t\ge f^\pi(x,z),\ (x,z)\in D^\pi\}\), then \(F\) is a projected perspective representation of the on-off epigraph. Eliminating \(y\) preserves the represented convex set, although it may replace a compact extended formulation by many inequalities or nonlinear constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected perspective formulation represents the perspective epigraph as the projection of an exact lifted convex set; eliminating auxiliaries preserves the set but may enlarge its description.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is closed and convex.
The stated projection equality holds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation of a positive-activation query point by a perspective cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((\bar x,\bar z,\bar t)\) with \(\bar z>0\), set \(u=\bar x/\bar z\), evaluate \(f(u)\), and choose \(g\in\partial f(u)\). The cut \[t\ge g^\top x+\bigl(f(u)-g^\top u\bigr)z\] has right-hand side \(\bar zf(u)\) at the query point. It is violated exactly when \(\bar t<\bar zf(\bar x/\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At positive activation, a subgradient at the normalized point generates an exact separating perspective cut.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.
A value and subgradient of \(f\) at \(\bar x/\bar z\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar t<\bar zf(\bar x/\bar z)\iff\text{the generated cut is violated.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Support-Point Cuts May Miss Boundary Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of using only subgradients at finite primal support points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The normalization \(u=x/z\) is unavailable at \(z=0\). A selected family of cuts generated only from finite points \(u\) need not expose every recession or domain restriction of the closed perspective. Exact zero-slice handling therefore requires the complete conjugate support family or separate enforcement of \(t\ge f^\infty(x)\) and the perspectivized domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-point subgradient cuts suffice for exact positive-activation separation but may omit zero-slice recession or domain restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z=0\text{ requires complete support or explicit recession/domain enforcement.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear halfspace representation of the closed perspective epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be closed, proper, and convex. For every \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\), \[t\ge y^\top x-zf^*(y)\] is valid for \(\operatorname{epi}f^\pi\). Moreover, for \(z\ge0\), the intersection of all these halfspaces is exactly \(\operatorname{epi}f^\pi\). If \(g\in\partial f(u)\), the indexed inequality becomes \[t\ge g^\top x+\bigl(f(u)-g^\top u\bigr)z.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All conjugate-indexed perspective cuts recover the closed perspective epigraph; subgradients give the familiar support-point form.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete Fenchel Perspective-Cut Family
Perspective-Cut Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane representation and separation of a closed perspective epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be closed proper convex. For any \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(g\in\partial f(u)\), the inequality \[t\ge g^\top x+\bigl(f(u)-g^\top u\bigr)z\] is valid for \(t\ge zf(x/z)\), \(z>0\), and remains valid for its closure. The intersection of all such inequalities, together with \(z\ge0\) and the perspectivized domain constraints, represents the closed perspective epigraph whenever supporting hyperplanes recover \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients of the original convex function generate linear perspective cuts; all such cuts recover the closed perspective epigraph under standard support representation conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex.
\(u\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(g\in\partial f(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge g^\top x+(f(u)-g^\top u)z\) is valid, and the complete cut family represents the closed perspective epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Off-State Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of a closed, unshifted perspective with an inactive state fixing the homogenized argument and nonlinear epigraph value at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let its closed perspective be \(\bar p_f(x,z)=z f(x/z)\) for \(z>0\), \(\bar p_f(x,0)=f^{\infty}(x)\), and \(\bar p_f(x,z)=+\infty\) for \(z<0\). Because \(f^{\infty}(0)=0\), the perspective epigraph at \(z=0\) and \(x=0\) is exactly \(\{(0,0,t):t\ge0\}\). Thus it is compatible with an inactive state prescribing zero argument and zero minimum nonlinear cost. Neither \(0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) nor \(f(0)=0\) is required for this boundary compatibility; those conditions concern evaluation or normalization of the active-state function at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed unshifted perspective exactly matches an off-state fixing the homogenized argument at zero and allowing epigraph cost at least zero, because every proper closed convex function has recession value zero in the zero direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The inactive state prescribes \(z=0\), \(x=0\), and \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed unshifted perspective is compatible with the prescribed inactive epigraph state because \(f^{\infty}(0)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compatibility Does Not Enforce a Singleton Off State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between a perspective accepting the prescribed inactive point and independently forcing that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed convex \(f\), the closed-perspective epigraph at \(z=0\) is \(\{(x,0,t):t\ge f^\infty(x)\}\). Hence \((x,t)=(0,t)\) with \(t\ge0\) is always compatible with the perspective, but the perspective constraint alone forces \(x=0\) at \(z=0\) if and only if \(f^\infty(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\). Otherwise a singleton inactive state requires an additional activation link or domain constraint excluding the nonzero finite-recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin is always a valid perspective off state, but it is the only finite off-state argument only when the function has no nonzero finite-cost recession direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The intended inactive state fixes the perspective argument at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility follows from \(f^\infty(0)=0\); automatic enforcement of \(x=0\) additionally requires \(\operatorname{dom}f^\infty=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed perspective of \(f\) is the extended-real-valued function
\[
\bar p_f(x,z)=\begin{cases}z f(x/z),&z>0,\\ f^{\infty}(x),&z=0,\\ +\infty,&z<0.\end{cases}
\]
It is the lower-semicontinuous closure of the ordinary perspective on \(z>0\). Consequently, zero activation need not force \(x=0\): a nonzero \(x\) is admitted at \(z=0\) precisely when the recession value \(f^{\infty}(x)\) is finite. If \(f\) has no nonzero finite-cost recession direction, only \(x=0\) has finite boundary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero scaling, the closed perspective equals the recession function, so nonzero boundary arguments survive exactly along finite-cost recession directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Writing \(v_i=f(t_i)\), continuity and affinity give
\[
\operatorname{gra} f=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\left\{\left((1-\lambda)t_{i-1}+\lambda t_i,(1-\lambda)v_{i-1}+\lambda v_i\right):0\le\lambda\le1\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, every \(x\in[t_{i-1},t_i]\) has the unique adjacent-breakpoint interpolation \(x=(1-\lambda)t_{i-1}+\lambda t_i\) and \(f(x)=(1-\lambda)v_{i-1}+\lambda v_i\). Consecutive graph segments share the point \((t_i,v_i)\), so no vertical connector or separate breakpoint disjunction is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous univariate piecewise-linear graph is the polygonal chain joining consecutive breakpoint-value pairs.

Its graph is a connected compact polygonal chain and therefore is closed in \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite continuous univariate piecewise-affine function is Lipschitz, and its graph is connected, compact, and closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is lower semicontinuous on \([a,b]\) if and only if, for every interior breakpoint \(t_i\),
\[
f(t_i)\le \min\{f(t_i-),f(t_i+)\},
\]
with the analogous one-sided inequality at each endpoint. Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi} f=\{(x,y):x\in[a,b],\ y\ge f(x)\}\) is closed. Strict inequality permits a downward isolated breakpoint value; an upward jump at the breakpoint violates lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-affine univariate function is lower semicontinuous exactly when no breakpoint value lies above an adjacent limiting value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph geometry of a finite lower-semicontinuous univariate piecewise-affine function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be lower semicontinuous and piecewise affine with finitely many breakpoints. Closing each affine interval at its limiting endpoint values and adding, at every breakpoint with a strictly lower assigned value, the ray \(\{t_i\}\times[f(t_i),\infty)\) yields exactly \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Hence the epigraph is a finite union of closed polyhedra. With rational breakpoint and affine data, it has an exact finite disjunctive mixed-integer linear representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph is a finite closed-polyhedral union, with a vertical ray accounting for each downward exceptional breakpoint value.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an interior breakpoint \(t_i\), continuity holds precisely when \(f(t_i-)=f(t_i)=f(t_i+)\). Thus \(f\) is discontinuous when this equality fails at some breakpoint. Its exact graph contains the affine pieces on their assigned open or half-open domains together with the selected point \((t_i,f(t_i))\); it does not contain an artificial vertical segment joining distinct limiting values. Consequently, the usual adjacent-breakpoint interpolation representation describes a continuous completion rather than the exact discontinuous graph and must be replaced by a disjunctive domain model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jump or exceptional breakpoint value makes adjacent-point interpolation inexact; the exact graph needs explicit disjunctive domain membership.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph Closure and Finite Closed-Disjunction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological obstruction to representing a genuinely discontinuous finite-valued graph by a finite closed-polyhedral disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-valued function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\), \(\operatorname{gra}f\) is closed if and only if \(f\) is continuous. Thus a genuinely discontinuous finite piecewise-affine graph is nonclosed; its closure contains the missing one-sided limiting graph points. Because the projection of each polyhedron is a polyhedron and a finite union of closed polyhedra is closed, such a graph cannot be represented as the projection of a finite closed-polyhedral disjunction, including a linear formulation with finitely bounded integer selectors and only non-strict inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discontinuous finite-valued graph on a compact interval is nonclosed and cannot equal a finite closed-polyhedral disjunction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is additively separable when
\[
f(x)=c+\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)
\]
for some constant \(c\). Introducing \(y_i=f_i(x_i)\) yields the exact extended representation
\[
y=c+\sum_{i=1}^n y_i,\qquad (x_i,y_i)\in\operatorname{gra} f_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).
\]
Hence each coordinate may use its own univariate piecewise-linear formulation. This decomposition is unavailable when a piece depends jointly on two or more coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additively separable multivariate function is modeled by independent univariate graphs whose values are summed.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Multivariate Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite-valued additively separable functions on convex product domains, convexity or concavity is exactly a coordinatewise property.

There are at most \(\prod_i m_i\) full-dimensional cells, whereas the separable extended graph representation uses the component formulations for only \(\sum_i m_i\) univariate pieces plus one aggregation equation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any simplex \(S\in\mathcal T\) and \(x\in S\), let the unique barycentric weights satisfy \(x=\sum_{p\in V(S)}\lambda_p p\), \(\sum_{p\in V(S)}\lambda_p=1\), and \(\lambda_p\ge0\). Define
\[
f(x)=\sum_{p\in V(S)}\lambda_p v_p.
\]
Agreement of vertex values on shared faces makes this definition independent of the containing simplex and continuous on \(D\). The resulting function is affine on each simplex but need not decompose by coordinate, so an exact formulation must select one simplex or an equivalent compatible face structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex values and barycentric interpolation over a triangulation define a continuous, generally nonseparable piecewise-affine function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A continuous polyhedral-complex function is a map \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[
f(x)=a_P^{\mathsf T}x+b_P\quad\text{for }x\in P,
\]
where, for every pair \(P,Q\in\mathcal P\), the two affine formulas agree on \(P\cap Q\). Its graph is
\[
\operatorname{gra} f=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{gra}(f|_P).
\]
The complex condition requires intersections to be common faces and every face of a cell to belong to \(\mathcal P\); unlike a triangulation, cells need not be simplices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral-complex function is affine on each compatible polyhedral cell, with neighboring formulas agreeing on shared faces.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Complex Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Compatibility Test on a Shared Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear-algebra test for agreement of neighboring affine formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonempty cells \(P,Q\) meet in the face \(F=P\cap Q\), choose \(x_0\in F\), and let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(F-F)\). Their affine formulas agree on all of \(F\) exactly when \[(a_P-a_Q)^{\mathsf T}x_0+b_P-b_Q=0\quad\text{and}\quad a_P-a_Q\in L^\perp.\] Equivalently, equality may be checked at any affine basis of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighboring affine formulas agree on a shared face exactly when their difference vanishes at one face point and along every face direction.
assumptions_latex: \(F=P\cap Q\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(P\in\mathcal P\), define \[\widehat P=\{(x,a_P^{\mathsf T}x+b_P):x\in P\}.\] If the cell formulas agree on all intersections, then the lifted cells, together with all their faces, form a polyhedral complex and \[\operatorname{gra}f=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}\widehat P.\] Projection onto \(x\) is an affine isomorphism from \(\widehat P\) to \(P\), preserving dimensions, faces, and incidences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifting every compatible affine cell produces a graph complex that is cellwise affinely isomorphic to the domain complex.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a finite polyhedral complex.
The affine formulas agree on every cell intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gra}f=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}\widehat P,\qquad \widehat{\mathcal P}\text{ is a polyhedral complex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is convex and piecewise affine if and only if there exist finitely many affine functions such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{k=1,\ldots,m}\{a_k^{\mathsf T}x+b_k\}\qquad(x\in D).
\]
Accordingly,
\[
\operatorname{epi} f=\{(x,y):x\in D,\ y\ge a_k^{\mathsf T}x+b_k\ \text{for all }k\}.
\]
Thus an epigraph constraint \(y\ge f(x)\) is represented exactly by linear inequalities and requires no piece-selection binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex piecewise-linear function is a finite maximum of affine functions, so its epigraph is described directly by linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Piecewise-Linear Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Both Global Affine Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous univariate example in neither the convex nor concave regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(D=[-2,2]\), let \(f\) interpolate \[(-2,0),\ (-1,1),\ (1,-1),\ (2,0).\] Its successive slopes are \(1,-1,1\), so it is neither convex nor concave. The segment affine extensions are \(\ell_1(x)=x+2\), \(\ell_2(x)=-x\), and \(\ell_3(x)=x-2\). At \(x=0\), \[f(0)=0,\qquad \max_i\ell_i(0)=2,\qquad \min_i\ell_i(0)=-2.\] Thus neither global envelope recovers the function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-segment function with slopes 1, -1, and 1 defeats both maximum-of-pieces and minimum-of-pieces representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph of a continuous convex piecewise-linear univariate function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a=x_0<x_1<\cdots <x_n=b\), let \(f_i\in\mathbb R\), and define \(m_i=(f_i-f_{i-1})/(x_i-x_{i-1})\). If \(m_1\le\cdots\le m_n\), the interpolant \(f\) is convex and
\[\operatorname{epi}(f)=\{(x,t)\in[a,b]\times\mathbb R:t\ge f_{i-1}+m_i(x-x_{i-1})\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\]
Thus its epigraph has an exact continuous linear-inequality representation; no segment-selection variables are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex piecewise-linear interpolant is the maximum of its segment affine extensions, so its epigraph is described by one linear lower bound per segment.

knowledge_statements.title: Lambda Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-combination representation of a continuous piecewise-linear graph using adjacent breakpoint weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For breakpoints \((x_j,f_j)\), where \(x_0<\cdots<x_n\), introduce \(\lambda_j\ge0\). The graph of their continuous piecewise-linear interpolant is represented by
\[x=\sum_{j=0}^n x_j\lambda_j,\qquad y=\sum_{j=0}^n f_j\lambda_j,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^n\lambda_j=1,\]
together with the requirement that the positive components of \(\lambda\) belong to some adjacent pair \(\{i-1,i\}\). Without this adjacency requirement, the system represents the convex hull of all breakpoint points rather than, in general, the interpolated graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lambda formulation for a univariate piecewise-linear function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interpolation on ordered breakpoints using adjacent-support lambda variables and a binary interval-selection encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a_1<\cdots<a_r and let f be piecewise linear on [a_1,a_r] with values f(a_i) at the breakpoints. For y\in[a_1,a_r], the exact graph relation is y=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i a_i and f(y)=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i f(a_i), where \lambda\ge 0, \sum_i\lambda_i=1, and \operatorname{supp}(\lambda) is contained in one adjacent pair \{j,j+1\}. This support condition is enforced by x\in\{0,1\}^{r-1}, \sum_{j=1}^{r-1}x_j=1, \lambda_1\le x_1, \lambda_i\le x_{i-1}+x_i\ (2\le i\le r-1), and \lambda_r\le x_{r-1}. Convex piecewise-linear functions can be minimized, and concave piecewise-linear functions maximized, by linear programming; representing the exact graph of a general piecewise-linear function requires segment selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex-combination weights represent a univariate piecewise-linear graph exactly when their positive support lies in one adjacent breakpoint pair. Binary interval variables enforce this condition. Convex minimization and concave maximization admit linear-programming formulations, whereas an exact general piecewise-linear graph requires segment selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Choice Segment Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-binary-per-segment formulation for a continuous piecewise-affine univariate graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let segment \(i\) have domain \([x_{i-1},x_i]\) and affine equation \(y=m_i x+b_i\). Introduce \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) and disaggregated \(u_i\). Then the graph union is represented by
\[\sum_{i=1}^n z_i=1,\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^n u_i,\qquad y=\sum_{i=1}^n(m_i u_i+b_i z_i),\qquad x_{i-1}z_i\le u_i\le x_i z_i.\]
Exactly one segment is active; its \(u_i\) equals \(x\), while all other disaggregated variables vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One binary chooses a segment, and a bounded disaggregated input variable enforces that segment's affine equation exactly.
