knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact segment-disaggregated convex-combination formulation for a piecewise-linear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each segment \(i\), introduce endpoint weights \(\lambda_i^-,\lambda_i^+\ge0\) and \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\). An exact formulation of the interpolated graph is
\[\lambda_i^-+\lambda_i^+=z_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n z_i=1,\]
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_{i-1}\lambda_i^-+x_i\lambda_i^+),\qquad y=\sum_{i=1}^n(f_{i-1}\lambda_i^-+f_i\lambda_i^+).\]
The selected segment contributes a convex combination of its endpoints, and every unselected segment has zero weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Incremental Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental formulation for a continuous piecewise-linear univariate graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d_i=x_i-x_{i-1}>0\) and \(g_i=f_i-f_{i-1}\). Introduce \(0\le\delta_i\le1\) and \(q_i\in\{0,1\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n-1\). The continuous interpolated graph is represented by
\[x=x_0+\sum_{i=1}^n d_i\delta_i,\qquad y=f_0+\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\delta_i,\]
\[\delta_{i+1}\le q_i\le\delta_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n-1).\]
Hence a later increment can be positive only after every preceding increment is full; at most one increment is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The input traverses segments in order: earlier increments are full, one current increment may be fractional, and later increments are zero.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0<\cdots<x_n\)
\(f\) is continuous and affine on every \([x_{i-1},x_i]\)

Lower-Semicontinuous Incremental Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why the ordinary incremental equations require modification at downward breakpoint jumps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let segment \(i\) have left and right endpoint ordinates \(f_i^-\) and \(f_i^+\), permitting \(f_i^-\ne f_i^+\) at breakpoint \(x_i\). The ordinary incremental identity
\[y=f_0+\sum_{i=1}^n(f_i-f_{i-1})\delta_i\]
is exact only when adjacent endpoint ordinates agree at every breakpoint. If \(f_i^-\ne f_i^+\), a single cumulative value at \(x_i\) cannot represent both incident limits. An exact lower-semicontinuous formulation must therefore disaggregate the incident segment states or introduce an explicit jump variable and enforce that the attained breakpoint value is the lower admissible value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard cumulative increments fail at discontinuities because one breakpoint ordinate cannot encode two incident limits; exact lower-semicontinuous models must represent jumps explicitly.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is affine on the interiors of consecutive breakpoint intervals
At least one breakpoint may have unequal incident limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding of segment adjacency using logarithmically many code coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_i\) denote the lambda vectors supported on \(\{i-1,i\}\), and assign each of the \(n\) segments a distinct code \(h^i\in\{0,1\}^k\), where \(k=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Define
\[Q=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n S_i\times\{h^i\}\right).\]
Then
\[\lambda\in\bigcup_{i=1}^nS_i\iff \exists z\in\mathbb Z^k:(\lambda,z)\in Q.\]
Together with the lambda equations for \(x\) and \(y\), this gives an exact piecewise-linear graph formulation using \(k\) binary encoding coordinates, provided a valid linear description of \(Q\) is imposed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\ge2\), let \(k=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\), and assign distinct codes \(h^i\in\{0,1\}^k\) to the segments \(i=1,\ldots,n\). In the common space of variables \(\lambda=(\lambda_1^-,\lambda_1^+,\ldots,\lambda_n^-,\lambda_n^+)\), define
\[D_i=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^{2n}:\lambda_i^-+\lambda_i^+=1,\ \lambda_j^-=\lambda_j^+=0\text{ for }j\ne i\}\]
and
\[Q_D=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^nD_i\times\{h^i\}\right).\]
Then
\[\lambda\in\bigcup_{i=1}^nD_i\iff\exists z\in\mathbb Z^k:(\lambda,z)\in Q_D.\]
With the global linear mapping
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_{i-1}\lambda_i^-+x_i\lambda_i^+),\qquad y=\sum_{i=1}^n(f_{i-1}\lambda_i^-+f_i\lambda_i^+),\]
this system represents exactly the continuous piecewise-linear graph.

Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) be nonempty polytopes, let \(H=\{h^1,\ldots,h^n\}\subseteq\mathbb Z^k\), and assume that the codes are in convex position, meaning that every \(h^i\) is a vertex of \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\). Assume also that the encoding is hole-free:

Then
\[x\in\bigcup_{i=1}^nP_i\iff\exists z\in\mathbb Z^k:(x,z)\in Q.\]
A complete linear description of \(Q\), together with integrality of \(z\), is an ideal extended formulation whose continuous relaxation is the convex hull of the embedded disjunction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive construction of an ordered logarithmic segment encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(G_0=(\epsilon)\). If \(G_{k-1}=(g^1,\ldots,g^{2^{k-1}})\), define \(G_k=(0g^1,\ldots,0g^{2^{k-1}},1g^{2^{k-1}},\ldots,1g^1)\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of the curvature-density rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(W=\int_a^b\sqrt{|f''(t)|}\,dt=0\), then \(f''\equiv0\), so \(f\) is affine and every mesh gives exact linear interpolation. knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional linear interpolation with fixed-sign, nonvanishing curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2([a,b])\) with either \(f''>0\) or \(f''<0\) on \([a,b]\), and put \(W=\int_a^b\sqrt{|f''(x)|}\,dx\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise, epigraph, and uniform-error certification from paired estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell,u:D\to\mathbb R\) be piecewise affine and satisfy \(\ell(x)\le f(x)\le u(x)\) on \(D\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact combinatorial growth under one-interval-at-a-time static splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from one interval, each split of a current interval increases the number of intervals and internal breakpoints by one. Thus after at most \(B\) splits the final partition has at most \(B+1\) intervals and \(B\) internal breakpoints. In a Cartesian construction with \(B_j+1\) intervals in coordinate \(j\), the number of cells is \(\prod_j(B_j+1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-at-a-time static split budget grows linearly in one dimension but multiplicatively in a tensor grid.
assumptions_latex: Each refinement replaces one interval by two nonempty child intervals.

Static Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Offline breakpoint refinement for a univariate factor in a factorable mixed-integer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a factor \(f:[\ell,u]\to\mathbb R\), a valid intervalwise error estimator \(E(I)\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and breakpoint budget \(B\), initialize \(\mathcal P=\{[\ell,u]\}\). While \(\max_{I\in\mathcal P}E(I)>\varepsilon\) and fewer than \(B\) breakpoints have been introduced, select an interval attaining the maximum estimator, insert a prescribed split point in that interval, and update \(\mathcal P\). Construct the piecewise-linear mixed-integer reformulation from the final partition and leave its breakpoints unchanged throughout optimization. The output is therefore fixed before branch-and-bound begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refine the largest-error intervals before optimization, stopping at a tolerance or breakpoint budget; the resulting piecewise-linear formulation remains fixed during the solve.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded on the finite interval \([\ell,u]\).
\(E(I)\) bounds the chosen approximation error uniformly on every interval \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\) and its resulting reformulation are fixed before the optimization search starts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of refinement rules triggered only by encountered relaxation solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rule that refines only the cell containing the current relaxation optimizer need not drive the maximum approximation error to zero: the optimizer sequence may repeatedly visit one region while another relevant cell with positive error is never refined. Global error convergence therefore requires an additional coverage condition, such as eventual refinement of every persistently positive-error relevant cell, or a global maximum-error selection rule.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive breakpoint generation driven by relaxation solutions encountered during mixed-integer search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a valid piecewise-linear relaxation with partitions \(\mathcal P_0\). At search iteration \(k\), solve the current node relaxation, obtaining \(x^k\). For every factor whose active interval \(I\in\mathcal P_k\) has certified local error exceeding \(\varepsilon\) at or around \(x^k\), insert a breakpoint in \(I\), add the corresponding valid linearization constraints, and set \(\mathcal P_{k+1}\) to the refined partitions. Continue branch-and-bound with all valid refinements retained. Stop when the search terminates or no inspected active interval violates the tolerance; return the incumbent and its final relaxation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: During search, relaxation solutions identify inaccurate active intervals; valid breakpoints and constraints are added there and retained until termination.
assumptions_latex: Every added linearization is valid for the original bounded factor domain.
The local error test is computable at each inspected relaxation solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_0\preceq\mathcal P_1\preceq\cdots\), and refinement locations depend on search information.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Bound Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity certificate for a bounded big-M linearization of one indicator implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty ambient domain for \(x\), let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and define \(Q=\{(x,z)\in D\times\{0,1\}:z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le 0\}\). The big-M system \(x\in D\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and \(g(x)\le M(1-z)\) represents exactly \(Q\) if and only if \(M\ge\sup_{x\in D}g(x)\). Consequently, any finite certified upper bound \(U\ge\sup_{x\in D}g(x)\) supplies the valid choice \(M=U\); if the supremum is infinite, no finite \(M\) exactly deactivates the inequality for every \(x\in D\) when \(z=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A big-M inequality represents the indicator implication over an ambient domain exactly when M bounds the deactivated expression throughout that domain; an infinite supremum precludes a finite valid M.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is nonempty.
\(z\) is binary.
\(g:D\to\mathbb R\) is defined throughout the ambient domain.

notation.meaning: Ambient domain for the original variables.
Feasible set defined by the indicator implication.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form finite-bound certificate for an affine indicator expression over a nonempty finite box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:L_i\le x_i\le U_i,\ i=1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(L_i,U_i\in\mathbb R\) and \(L_i\le U_i\), and let \(g(x)=a^\top x-b\). Then \[\sup_{x\in D}g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\max\{a_iL_i,a_iU_i\}-b.\] Consequently, this value is the smallest valid constant in \(g(x)\le M(1-z)\) for the implication \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\) over \(D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Point Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness restricted to feasible assignments of the original integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be an original feasible set, let \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) index its integer-constrained coordinates, and let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) be a reformulation with auxiliary variables \(y\), including any required integrality restrictions. The reformulation is integer-point equivalent to \(X\) when
\[\{x\in X:x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|}\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|},\ \exists y\text{ with }(x,y)\in R\}.\]
Thus it neither removes nor introduces feasible original-variable points satisfying the designated integrality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reformulation is integer-point equivalent when its projected feasible points with designated original coordinates integral exactly match those of the original model.
assumptions_latex: The same original-variable integrality index set \(J\) is used on both sides.
All auxiliary-variable restrictions are included in \(R\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the extended reformulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion certificate schema for exactness on designated integer original points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Integer-point equivalence holds if and only if (i) every \(x\in X\) with \(x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|}\) admits \(y\) with \((x,y)\in R\), and (ii) every \((x,y)\in R\) with \(x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|}\) satisfies \(x\in X\). A witness violating either direction certifies nonequivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactness on designated integer points is certified by liftability of every original integer-feasible point and soundness of every lifted point with integral designated original coordinates.
assumptions_latex: All original- and auxiliary-variable restrictions are included in \(X\) and \(R\).
The same original integrality index set \(J\) is used in both directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer-Point Equivalence Does Not Imply Projection Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[0,1]\), \(J=\{1\}\), and \(R=\{(x,y):x\in\{0,1\},\ y=0\}\). Then \(X\cap\mathbb Z=\{0,1\}=\operatorname{proj}_x(R)\cap\mathbb Z\), but \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\{0,1\}\ne X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reformulation can preserve exactly the integral original points while omitting fractional points of the original feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The sole original coordinate is designated integer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequence for objectives depending only on original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(R\) is integer-point equivalent to \(X\) for \(J\), then every objective \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) depending only on \(x\) has the same attainable values on the two projected integer-feasible sets. Consequently their infima, attainment status, and optimal original-variable points coincide; auxiliary optimizers may be nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer-point-equivalent reformulations preserve every original-variable objective on the designated mixed-integer domain.
assumptions_latex: The projected integer-feasible original-variable sets are equal.
The objective depends only on original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in X,\ x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|}}f(x)=\inf_{(x,y)\in R,\ x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|}}f(x).

notation.meaning: objective depending only on original variables

knowledge_statements.title: Original-Objective Preservation on Integer Points

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation under a common original-variable domain and integrality convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=X\), then for every \(J\subseteq[n]\), \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)\cap\{x:x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|}\}=X\cap\{x:x_J\in\mathbb Z^{|J|}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full projection equivalence gives integer-point equivalence for every choice of designated original integer coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=X\).
The same coordinates \(J\) and integrality convention are used on both sides.

notation.meaning: indices of designated integer original variables

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Equivalence Implies Integer-Point Equivalence
Projection Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full feasible-set exactness after eliminating auxiliary reformulation variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the original feasible set and let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) contain every constraint and integrality restriction of an extended reformulation. The reformulation is projection equivalent to \(X\) precisely when
\[\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q\text{ such that }(x,y)\in R\}=X.\]
This condition requires equivalence for all original-variable feasible points, not merely for points at which selected original coordinates happen to be integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection equivalence holds when eliminating all auxiliary variables from the reformulation yields exactly the original feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) includes all continuous and discrete restrictions of the reformulation.
Projection eliminates only auxiliary variables \(y\).

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming
source_refs.locator: 2.5 Extended block-separable reformulation p. 17

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming
source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Extended block-separable reformulation p. 17

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical inclusion certificate for equality after eliminating auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Projection equivalence holds if and only if (i) every \(x\in X\) admits some \(y\) with \((x,y)\in R\), and (ii) every \((x,y)\in R\) satisfies \(x\in X\). A point violating either direction certifies nonequivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection equality is certified by completeness of lifting and soundness of every lifted feasible point.
assumptions_latex: All constraints and integrality restrictions of the extended model are included in \(R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Direction Projection-Equivalence Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Projection Validity Is Not Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that either projection inclusion alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[0,1]\). The set \(R_{\mathrm{out}}=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le2,\ y=0\}\) satisfies \(X\subsetneq\operatorname{proj}_x(R_{\mathrm{out}})\), while \(R_{\mathrm{in}}=\{(x,y):x\in\{0,1\},\ y=0\}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_{\mathrm{in}})\subsetneq X\). Neither is projection equivalent to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer lift may introduce original points and an inner lift may remove them; either single inclusion falls short of projection equivalence.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Projection Validity Is Not Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure under successive introduction and elimination of auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) satisfy \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_1)=X\). If \(R_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\times\mathbb R^r\) satisfies \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(R_2)=R_1\), then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_2)=X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive exact lifts remain projection equivalent after eliminating every auxiliary layer.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_1)=X\).
\(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(R_2)=R_1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Exact Lifts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequence for objectives defined on original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=X\), then for every \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the attainable value sets \(\{f(x):x\in X\}\) and \(\{f(x):(x,y)\in R\}\) coincide. Hence their infima, attainment status, and optimal original-variable points coincide; auxiliary representations may be nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection-equivalent formulations preserve every objective depending only on original variables.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=X\).
The objective depends only on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Objective Invariance under Projection Equivalence
Ideal Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard vertex-integrality definition for a bounded mixed-integer linear extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) be the polyhedral relaxation of an exact mixed-integer formulation, and let \(K\) index every variable required to be integral in that formulation. The formulation is ideal if every extreme point \(v\in\operatorname{ext}(R)\) satisfies \(v_K\in\mathbb Z^{|K|}\). Equivalently, for a polytope \(R\),
\[R=\operatorname{conv}\{v\in R:v_K\in\mathbb Z^{|K|}\}.\]
Hence optimizing any linear objective over the continuous relaxation has an integral optimal extreme point whenever an optimum exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact bounded formulation is ideal when every vertex of its continuous relaxation is integral in all variables designated as integer.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a polytope obtained by relaxing the designated integrality restrictions.
The mixed-integer formulation is exact for its intended feasible set.

notation.meaning: Indices of all designated integer variables.

source_refs.source_title: Integer Programming
source_refs.locator: 1.7 Good and Ideal Formulations p. 15

source_witnesses.source_title: Integer Programming
source_witnesses.locator: 1.7 Good and Ideal Formulations p. 15

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded exact formulations; relation from lifted-space ideality to original-space sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+q}\) be the relaxation polytope of an exact formulation, let \(K\) contain all integer-designated coordinates, and set \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x(R\cap\{v:v_K\in\mathbb Z^{|K|}\})\). If every vertex of \(R\) is integral on \(K\), then \[\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{conv}(S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bounded exact ideal formulation is sharp in the original-variable space.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a polytope.
The formulation is exact after imposing all designated integrality restrictions.
Every vertex of \(R\) is integral on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.title: Ideality Implies Projected Hull Exactness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal lifted-space separation between projected sharpness and vertex integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^2:x\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ x+2z\le1\}\), with both \(x\) and \(z\) designated integer in the exact formulation. Its integer-feasible projection is \(S=\{0,1\}\), while \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=[0,1]=\operatorname{conv}(S)\). Thus the formulation is sharp, but it is not ideal because \((0,\tfrac12)\) is a fractional vertex of \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation can have the exact projected hull while retaining a fractional vertex in an integer-designated auxiliary coordinate.
assumptions_latex: Both coordinates are integer-designated before relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Does Not Imply Ideality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull exactness after projecting an exact extended relaxation onto the designated original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the represented feasible set and let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+q}\) be the continuous relaxation of an exact extended formulation. The formulation is sharp in \(x\)-space when \[\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{conv}(S).\] Sharpness concerns this projection and does not require integrality of vertices in the lifted space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation is sharp when its continuous relaxation projects exactly to the convex hull of the represented set.
assumptions_latex: The unrelaxed formulation projects exactly onto \(S\).
The original-variable projection \(\operatorname{proj}_x\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Hull Definition of Sharpness
Sharp Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull exactness measured after projecting the continuous extended relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set represented in original-variable space, and let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) be the continuous relaxation of an exact extended formulation. The formulation is sharp in the original-variable space if
\[\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{conv}(S).\]
Sharpness concerns the projected relaxation and therefore does not require every extreme point of \(R\) itself to satisfy the formulation's auxiliary integrality restrictions. An ideal formulation is sharp under exactness, but a sharp extended formulation need not be ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation is sharp when projecting its continuous relaxation onto original variables gives exactly the convex hull of the represented feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is the relaxation obtained by dropping designated integrality restrictions.
The unrelaxed formulation projects exactly onto \(S\).

notation.meaning: Represented feasible set in original-variable space.

source_refs.source_title: Integer Programming
source_refs.locator: 1.7 Good and Ideal Formulations p. 15

source_witnesses.source_title: Integer Programming
source_witnesses.locator: 1.7 Good and Ideal Formulations p. 15

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected convex-hull condition is mathematically coherent, but the cited section on good and ideal formulations does not reliably establish that this exact condition is called sharp or support the stated ideal-versus-sharp comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Hereditarily Sharp Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness required to survive every feasible fixing of designated discrete variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) be an exact extended formulation of \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with designated discrete coordinates indexed by \(K\). For \(F\subseteq K\) and every feasible integral assignment \(a\) to \(F\), define the corresponding faces \(R(F,a)=R\cap\{v:v_F=a\}\) and \(S(F,a)=S\cap\{x:x_{F\cap\{1,\ldots,n\}}=a_{F\cap\{1,\ldots,n\}}\}\), with auxiliary fixings interpreted through the extended model. The formulation is hereditarily sharp when every such restricted formulation satisfies
\[\operatorname{proj}_x(R(F,a))=\operatorname{conv}(S(F,a)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation is hereditarily sharp when sharpness remains valid after every feasible integral fixing of any subset of its designated discrete variables.
assumptions_latex: The unrelaxed extended formulation projects exactly onto \(S\).
Only feasible integral assignments to designated discrete variables are considered.

notation.meaning: Relaxation restricted by a partial integral assignment.
Represented set under the corresponding fixing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and the treatment of fixings of auxiliary discrete variables through S(F,a) is not formally defined. The exact hereditary-sharpness convention therefore remains unreliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-formulation size measured by variables added beyond the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an extended formulation \(R=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q:A x+B y\le b\}\) of a set in \(x\)-space, its auxiliary-variable complexity is \(q\), optionally reported as the pair \((q_c,q_d)\) counting added continuous and discrete variables separately. For a prescribed formulation class \(\mathcal F\), the minimum auxiliary-variable complexity is
\[\operatorname{avc}_{\mathcal F}(S)=\min\{q:R\in\mathcal F\text{ is an admissible formulation of }S\}.\]
Original variables are excluded, while every introduced copy, selector, epigraph, and product variable is counted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary-variable complexity counts variables introduced beyond the original model; minimizing this count over an admissible class defines the class-relative measure.
assumptions_latex: The original-variable vector \(x\) is fixed in advance.
The admissible formulation class \(\mathcal F\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{avc}(R)=q\), with \(\operatorname{avc}_{\mathcal F}(S)\) obtained by minimizing over admissible formulations.

source_refs.source_title: Integer Programming
source_refs.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

source_witnesses.source_title: Integer Programming
source_witnesses.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary count is presentation-dependent unless minimized under a fixed admissibility convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(R=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le b\}\), then adjoining \(z\in\mathbb R^k\) and \(z=0\) gives an equivalent extension \(R'\) satisfying \[\operatorname{proj}_x(R')=\operatorname{proj}_x(R),\qquad \operatorname{avc}(R')=\operatorname{avc}(R)+k.\] Hence displayed auxiliary count is not invariant under equivalent presentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulations can contain arbitrarily many redundant auxiliary variables.
assumptions_latex: Fixed auxiliary variables are allowed.
The original variables and projection map are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Presentation Dependence of Auxiliary Count
Inequality Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-formulation size measured by the number of linear inequality rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedral extended formulation \(R=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le b,\ Cx+Dy=d\}\), define its inequality complexity under the convention that equations are recorded separately to be the number \(m\) of rows of \(Ax+By\le b\). This count is specific to the displayed representation and includes redundant inequality rows if they are present. For a polytope \(P\), its extension complexity is \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{m:\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=P\text{ for a polyhedron }R\text{ admitting a description with }m\text{ inequalities}\}.\] Thus extension complexity minimizes inequality count across all linear extensions, whereas the inequality complexity of one displayed formulation need not be minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inequality complexity of a displayed formulation is its number of inequality rows under a fixed convention that records equations separately; extension complexity minimizes this count over all linear extensions.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a polyhedral formulation.
Equations are recorded separately and are not included in \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min_R\{\text{number of inequalities in a description of }R:\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=P\}\).

notation.meaning: Number of inequality rows in the selected description.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical factorization characterization of minimum inequality count for polytope extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polytope with at least two points and let \(M_P\) be any vertex-facet slack matrix. Under the convention that equations are free and only inequalities are counted, \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(M_P),\] where \(\operatorname{rank}_+\) is nonnegative rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope's extension complexity equals the nonnegative rank of its slack matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polytope with at least two points.
Equations are not included in the inequality count.
knowledge_statements.title: Slack-Matrix Characterization of Extension Complexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet Count as Minimum Original-Space Inequality Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original-space benchmark for inequality complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty polytope considered in its affine hull, and let \(f(P)\) denote its number of facets. Every exact original-space inequality description contains at least \(f(P)\) nonredundant inequalities, and an irredundant facet description contains exactly \(f(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum original-space inequality count of a polytope is its facet count.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polytope.
Equations defining \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\) are counted separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{m:P\text{ has an original-space description with }m\text{ inequalities}\}=f(P)\).

notation.meaning: Number of facets relative to the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet Count as Minimum Original-Space Inequality Count
Encoding Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary description length of a rational linear or mixed-integer reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational formulation specified by coefficient data \(\mathcal D=(A,B,C,D,b,d)\), variable types, and finite rational bounds, its encoding complexity \(L(\mathcal D)\) is the total number of bits in a fixed binary representation of all dimensions, indices, signs, numerators, and denominators after each rational is written in reduced form. Two formulations with equal row and variable counts may therefore have different encoding complexity. Polynomial-size reformulation claims require \(L(\mathcal D)\) to be polynomial in the input encoding length, rather than requiring only polynomially many rows and variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding complexity is the total binary description length of rational coefficients, bounds, indices, dimensions, and variable types, not merely the number of rows or variables.
assumptions_latex: All numerical formulation data are rational and finitely represented.
A fixed reasonable binary coding convention is used.

notation.meaning: Complete rational coefficient and bound data.
Binary encoding length of the formulation.
Bit length of a reduced rational datum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robustness of polynomial-size claims under mutually efficient finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_1,L_2\) encode the same finite rational formulation data, and suppose each encoding can be translated into the other in polynomial time. Then polynomials \(p,q\) exist such that \[L_2(\mathcal D)\le p(L_1(\mathcal D)),\qquad L_1(\mathcal D)\le q(L_2(\mathcal D)).\] Thus polynomial encoding size is invariant under these coding conventions, although exact bit counts are not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mutually polynomial-time translatable encodings preserve polynomial-size formulation claims.
assumptions_latex: Both encodings represent the same finite rational data.
Translations in both directions are polynomial-time.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Equivalence of Reasonable Encodings

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition for selecting auxiliary representatives without deleting projected solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) of reformulation-induced symmetries act on \(R\), and let \(B\subseteq R\) intersect every \(G\)-orbit in \(R\). Because every element of \(G\) fixes \(x\), \[\operatorname{proj}_x(B)=\operatorname{proj}_x(R).\] Thus constraints defining such a representative set may remove duplicate auxiliary encodings without removing an original-variable solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry-breaking constraints preserve the original projection when they retain at least one representative from every auxiliary orbit.
assumptions_latex: Every transformation in \(G\) fixes the original variables.
\(B\) intersects every orbit of \(G\) on \(R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Preserving Symmetry Breaking

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example separating reformulation-induced symmetry from symmetry of original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x,y_1,y_2\in\{0,1\}\) with \(y_1+y_2=x\). Swapping \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) fixes \(x\) and preserves the formulation. The projected solution \(x=1\) has the two auxiliary encodings \((y_1,y_2)=(1,0)\) and \((0,1)\). Adding \(y_1\ge y_2\) retains one encoding for every feasible \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single original solution can have two interchangeable auxiliary encodings even when the original variable is fixed.
assumptions_latex: All three variables are binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1,0)\leftrightarrow(0,1)\) is a nontrivial auxiliary symmetry for \(x=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Duplicate Auxiliary Encoding Example

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetries created by interchangeable auxiliary representations while original variables remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq X\times Y\) be an extended reformulation with objective \(c\). A reformulation-induced symmetry is a nonidentity bijection \(\sigma:Y\to Y\) preserving domains and variable types such that, for every \((x,y)\), \[(x,y)\in R\iff(x,\sigma(y))\in R,\qquad c(x,y)=c(x,\sigma(y)).\] It fixes every original coordinate and maps auxiliary encodings of the same projected solution to one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reformulation-induced symmetry changes only auxiliary encodings while preserving feasibility and objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(\sigma\) preserves auxiliary domains and integrality types.
The objective is defined on the extended space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y)\mapsto(x,\sigma(y))\) preserves feasibility, objective value, and the original-variable projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Fixing Reformulation Symmetry
Reformulation-Induced Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry created by interchangeable auxiliary encodings while original variables remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\subseteq X\times Y\) be an extended reformulation. A reformulation-induced symmetry is a nonidentity bijection \(\sigma:Y\to Y\), typically a permutation of auxiliary coordinates or encoding labels, such that
\[(x,y)\in R\iff(x,\sigma(y))\in R\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y,\]
and the objective value is unchanged under \((x,y)\mapsto(x,\sigma(y))\). Such a symmetry fixes every original variable while mapping one auxiliary representation of the same original solution to another. The set of all such transformations is a group under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reformulation-induced symmetry permutes auxiliary encodings, fixes original variables, and preserves feasibility and objective value, thereby creating equivalent extended solutions.
assumptions_latex: The objective is defined on the extended variable space.
\(\sigma\) preserves the domains and integrality types of auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proposed interval \([L,U]\) for a source expression \(v\) is valid on \(D\) if and only if \(L\le v(x)\le U\) for every \(x\in D\). Validation may use optimization certificates \(L\le\inf_{x\in D}v(x)\) and \(U\ge\sup_{x\in D}v(x)\). If a downstream big-\(M\), McCormick, or disjunctive linearization requires finite endpoints, validity additionally requires \(L,U\in\mathbb{R}\). Bounds inherited from a larger domain remain valid on \(D\), whereas bounds computed on a strict subdomain are not globally valid without preserving that domain restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source bounds must enclose every attainable expression value on their deployment domain; locally derived bounds cannot be used outside that domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Source-Bound Validation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp consequence of a source interval omitting an attainable value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a reformulation enforces \(L\le v\le U\), but there exists \(\bar x\in D\) with \(v(\bar x)<L\) or \(v(\bar x)>U\). The exact lift associated with \(\bar x\) then violates the reformulation, so it is not a relaxation of the original domain and may delete a feasible or optimal solution. Enlarging a valid interval preserves validity but may weaken a bound-dependent envelope; shrinking it without certification may invalidate the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source interval omitting one attainable value can delete a feasible or optimal point, while an overly wide valid interval merely weakens the formulation.
assumptions_latex: The reformulation enforces the declared source interval.
An attainable source value lies outside that interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reformulation is invalid on the declared deployment domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sound inclusion-isotonic range propagation through a finite acyclic expression graph produces valid intervals for its intermediate expressions and root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sound expression-graph propagation can produce valid source bounds.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
Input intervals and every elemental range rule are valid.

knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation-Aware Bound Tightening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-based tightening that includes the deployed reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set, let \(w=(w_i)_{i\in I}\) be the reformulation variables, and initialize valid finite intervals \([L_i^0,U_i^0]\) for every \(i\in I\). At iteration \(k\), construct a nonempty relaxation \(R_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^{I}\) in variables \((x,w)\) using the original constraints, the current intervals, and all deployed reformulation constraints. For each selected \(i\in I\), compute certified values \(\ell_i^k\le\inf\{w_i:(x,w)\in R_k\}\) and \(u_i^k\ge\sup\{w_i:(x,w)\in R_k\}\), and set \(L_i^{k+1}=\max\{L_i^k,\ell_i^k\}\) and \(U_i^{k+1}=\min\{U_i^k,u_i^k\}\); leave unselected intervals unchanged. Stop when no selected interval improves beyond the prescribed tolerance or a resource limit is reached, and return the last valid intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from valid finite intervals, repeatedly optimize selected reformulation variables over the current reformulation-aware relaxation, intersect certified results with the existing intervals, and stop when tightening stalls or a resource limit is reached.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite index set and \(w=(w_i)_{i\in I}\) denotes the reformulation variables.
For every iteration \(k\), \(R_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^{I}\) is a nonempty valid relaxation of the current bounded-domain formulation.
Every auxiliary bound subproblem returns certified valid lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\in I\), validity is preserved and \([L_i^{k+1},U_i^{k+1}]\subseteq[L_i^k,U_i^k]\).

notation.meaning: finite index set of reformulation variables
current bounds for reformulation variable i
certified candidate lower and upper bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound infeasibility detection during reformulation-aware tightening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every exact feasible lift belongs to the current relaxation \(R_k\). A certified proof that \(R_k=\varnothing\) proves infeasibility of the original bounded-domain formulation. Likewise, if independently certified valid lower and upper bounds yield \(L_i>U_i\) for some reformulation variable, no exact feasible lift exists. Solver failure, an uncertified objective bound, or an unbounded auxiliary objective alone proves neither conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified relaxation infeasibility or contradictory certified bounds prove infeasibility; failed or uncertified bound solves do not.
assumptions_latex: \(R_k\) contains every exact feasible lift.
Every endpoint used in an interval contradiction is certified on the same deployment domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Infeasibility and Empty-Interval Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-sweep optimization count and absence of unconditional finite convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one sweep computes both extrema separately for every variable in \(J\subseteq I\), it requires at most \(2|J|\) auxiliary optimization solves. Fewer are needed when only one endpoint is requested or an endpoint is already fixed. The produced interval sequence is nested, but monotonicity does not imply finite exact convergence: rebuilding relaxations can produce an infinite strictly tightening sequence. A practical algorithm therefore needs a tolerance, pass or resource limit, or a structural finite-state condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-sided sweep uses at most two bound solves per selected variable, and nested tightening need not converge finitely.
assumptions_latex: Each requested endpoint is computed by a separate auxiliary optimization problem.
Relaxations may be rebuilt after interval changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A two-sided sweep uses at most \(2|J|\) solves; finite exact termination requires an explicit rule or additional structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Sweep Cost and Finite-Convergence Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable data needed to install and inherit a bound-dependent local reformulation safely.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deployment certificate for \(R_N\) records the node-domain restrictions, every local cut or assumption used, each bound-dependent coefficient and its certified source interval, and the subtree scope in which those assumptions remain valid. Any change that relaxes a recorded assumption requires revalidation before reuse; strengthening to a descendant domain permits inheritance or certified rebuilding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safe deployment records the node domain and every local assumption and bound on which the reformulation depends.
assumptions_latex: The reformulation contains coefficients or constraints derived from node-local data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate makes the validity domain and permitted inheritance of each local component checkable.
knowledge_statements.title: Deployment-Scope Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and inheritance boundary for a reformulation generated inside a search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_N\) be a node domain and let \(R_N\) be an extended relaxation such that every original feasible point in \(D_N\) has a feasible lift in \(R_N\). Then \(R_N\) is valid at node \(N\), and every constraint of \(R_N\) remains valid at a descendant \(M\) whenever \(D_M\subseteq D_N\). It is not automatically valid at an ancestor or a different branch. Bound-dependent constraints may be rebuilt with tighter bounds certified on \(D_M\), but rebuilding preserves relaxation validity only when every original feasible point in \(D_M\) still has a lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-local reformulation is valid on its certified node domain and inherited subdomains, but not automatically on ancestors or sibling branches.
assumptions_latex: Every original feasible point in \(D_N\) has a feasible lift in \(R_N\).
A descendant satisfies \(D_M\subseteq D_N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_N\) remains a valid relaxation on \(D_M\), with no automatic validity outside \(D_N\).
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Domain Validity and Descendant Inheritance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure when a locally tightened source interval is exported outside its certified branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose branch \(N\) implies \(v(x)\le U_N\), and a local reformulation enforces that bound. If another branch contains a feasible point \(\bar x\) with \(v(\bar x)>U_N\), installing the local reformulation there deletes the exact lift of \(\bar x\). Thus subtree containment, not merely common ancestry or a shared algebraic expression, is required for automatic inheritance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exporting a branch-specific bound to a branch containing a larger attainable value can cut off a feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(U_N\) is valid only on \(D_N\).
Another branch contains an attainable value exceeding \(U_N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transferred reformulation is invalid on the other branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Cross-Branch Transfer

assumptions_latex: A branch-and-bound node has domain \(D_N\subseteq D\).
All local bounds and cuts are valid throughout \(D_N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local reformulation is valid on \(D_N\) and may be inherited only by descendants whose domains lie in \(D_N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and inheritance boundary for reformulations generated inside search.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_N\) be constructed from constraints valid on \(D_N\), including linearizations parameterized by bounds certified on \(D_N\). Then every original feasible point in \(D_N\) has a feasible lift in \(R_N\), so \(R_N\) is a valid node relaxation. If a descendant \(M\) satisfies \(D_M\subseteq D_N\), the same constraints remain valid on \(D_M\). They must not be installed at an ancestor or unrelated node unless their bounds and cuts are independently validated there. Rebuilding envelopes with tighter descendant bounds can strengthen the relaxation without changing integer-feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reformulation built from node-valid bounds is valid for that node and its descendants, but not automatically elsewhere in the search tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Local Reformulations

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Linear Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended linear representation assembled from factor-level formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite acyclic expression graph whose leaves are the original variables \(x\), and introduce an auxiliary variable \(w_v\) for every internal node \(v\in V_{\mathrm{int}}\). For each \(v\in V_{\mathrm{int}}\), impose a linear or mixed-integer linear set \(P_v\) that is either an exact extended formulation of the relation between \(w_v\) and its child variables or an outer approximation of that relation on their stated domains. Form \(P\) by intersecting all \(P_v\), the original linear constraints, the root constraints, the variable domains, and all declared integrality restrictions, using shared variables consistently across factors. If every \(P_v\) is exact on its deployment domain, then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\) equals the original feasible set. If every \(P_v\) is valid and at least one is only an outer approximation, then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\) contains the original feasible set and is a valid relaxation, without an implied equality claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent every required expression-graph relation with consistent auxiliary variables and linear constraints. Exact factor formulations yield an exact extended representation, while valid outer approximations yield a valid relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite acyclic expression graph containing every expression relation required by the original constraints.
Each internal node \(v\in V_{\mathrm{int}}\) has an auxiliary variable \(w_v\), and shared child variables are identified consistently across factor formulations.
Each \(P_v\) is exact or is a valid outer approximation on the stated source domain, and the assembled system includes the original root constraints, domains, and integrality restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every \(P_v\) is exact, then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\) equals the original feasible set; if the factors are merely valid outer approximations, then the original feasible set is contained in \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\).

notation.meaning: auxiliary variable for internal node v
factor-level linear or mixed-integer linear representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive Size of Factorwise Linear Assembly
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row, auxiliary-variable, and encoding-size accounting for direct factorwise assembly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an explicitly represented acyclic expression graph have internal nodes \(V_{\mathrm{int}}\). Suppose the factor formulation for node \(v\) contributes \(r_v\) scalar rows, \(q_v\) private auxiliary variables beyond shared node and child variables, and description length \(L_v\). If the original linear system contributes \(r_0\) rows and length \(L_0\), direct intersection uses \(r_0+\sum_v r_v\) scalar rows and \(|V_{\mathrm{int}}|+\sum_v q_v\) added variables. Under a fixed sparse indexing convention its description length is at most \(L_0+\sum_vL_v+O(|V|+|E|)\). Hence polynomial-size factor formulations produce a polynomial-size assembled representation when the explicit expression graph is polynomial in size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct factorwise assembly has additive row, auxiliary-variable, and encoding size and remains polynomial when its graph and factors are polynomially represented.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite explicitly represented acyclic expression graph.
Private factor auxiliaries are distinct, while node and child variables are shared consistently.
A fixed sparse encoding and counting convention is used.

notation.meaning: scalar rows contributed by factor v
private auxiliary variables contributed by factor v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent feasible-set semantics of a one-way linear indicator constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\). The indicator \(z=b\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) denotes \(\{(x,z):z\ne b\}\cup\{(x,z):z=b,\ a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\}\), intersected with the remaining model domain. It imposes no restriction from this row when \(z\ne b\), and it is not the biconditional \(z=b\Leftrightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator enforces its row at one binary value and imposes nothing by itself at the other; it is a one-way implication, not an equivalence.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Constraint Semantics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator Semantics Do Not Determine a Fractional Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between an indicator's integer-fiber contract and a solver's chosen compilation or relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(0\le x\le1\) with \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the indicator \(z=1\Rightarrow x\le0\) is represented exactly at binary \(z\) by either \(x\le1-z\) or \(x\le2(1-z)\). After relaxing \(z\in[0,1]\), the first requires \(x\le1/2\) at \(z=1/2\), while the second permits every \(x\le1\). Thus the logical indicator contract determines its integer fibers but not a unique continuous relaxation, branching implementation, or numerical strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations can implement the same binary indicator yet have different fractional relaxations; native indicator syntax alone does not specify relaxation strength.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in\{0,1\}\) for semantic equivalence and \(z\in[0,1]\) for the relaxation comparison.

notation.meaning: system with x at most 1-z and the base bounds
system with x at most 2(1-z) and the base bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent reductions among common linear indicator forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the data of Indicator-Constraint Semantics, \(z=b\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x=\beta\) is equivalent to the conjunction \(z=b\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) and \(z=b\Rightarrow-a^{\mathsf T}x\le-\beta\). Setting \(z'=1-z\) converts activation at \(b=0\) into activation at \(z'=1\) without changing the represented pairs after substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicated equality is two indicated inequalities, and complementing the binary variable converts zero activation into one activation.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indicator constraint \(z=b\Rightarrow a^\top x\le\beta\) denotes the feasible set \(\{(x,z):z\in\{0,1\},\ z\ne b\}\cup\{(x,z):z=b,\ a^\top x\le\beta\}\), intersected with all other model constraints. When \(z\ne b\), this indicator alone imposes no restriction on \(a^\top x\). The implication is therefore not the biconditional \(z=b\Leftrightarrow a^\top x\le\beta\). Any explicit big-\(M\) translation must use a valid bound on the maximum violation of the indicated inequality over the inactive-state domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical SOS1 semantics, excluding solver tolerances and branching policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A special ordered set of type 1 on \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) imposes \(|\operatorname{supp}(v)|\le1\), where \(\operatorname{supp}(v)=\{i:v_i\ne0\}\). Thus all members may be zero, or exactly one member may be nonzero. Weights supplied with the set identify members and may define an ordering for solver operations, but ordering is not part of the SOS1 feasibility predicate. Numerical solvers generally interpret nonzero status using implementation tolerances; those tolerances belong to the solver interface rather than the exact mathematical set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS1 permits at most one member to be nonzero; member weights do not alter this exact feasibility condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SOS2 Singleton and Adjacent-Pair Edge Cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified exact support condition covering nonempty SOS2 lists, including the one-member case omitted by the adjacent-pair formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered nonempty list \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) with \(m\ge1\), SOS2 feasibility is equivalently expressed by requiring \(\operatorname{supp}(v)\) to be contained in a consecutive index block of cardinality at most two. If \(m=1\), this permits exactly the empty support and \(\{1\}\). If \(m\ge2\), it is equivalent to \(\operatorname{supp}(v)\subseteq\{j,j+1\}\) for some \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\). Whether a particular solver accepts a one-member SOS2 declaration is an implementation issue, not a change to this mathematical convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contiguous-support definition covers a one-member SOS2; the usual adjacent-pair formula is equivalent only when at least two members exist.
assumptions_latex: The SOS members have an unambiguous linear order.
knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Singleton and Adjacent-Pair Edge Cases

assumptions_latex: \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) are ordered by distinct weights \(\omega_1<\cdots<\omega_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: SOS2 feasibility requires \(\operatorname{supp}(v)\subseteq\{j,j+1\}\) for some admissible index \(j\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-support semantics used by piecewise-linear formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A special ordered set of type 2 on members \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\), ordered by weights \(\omega_1<\cdots<\omega_m\), requires that at most two members be nonzero and, when two are nonzero, their indices be consecutive. Equivalently, \(\operatorname{supp}(v)\subseteq\{j,j+1\}\) for some \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\), with the empty and singleton supports also feasible. The weights determine adjacency and therefore must induce an unambiguous order. SOS2 semantics alone impose neither normalization nor interpolation equations such as \(\sum_i v_i=1\); those must be modeled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS2 permits nonzeros only among one adjacent pair in the weight order; normalization and interpolation equations are separate constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent correctness condition for translating an SOS interface into a possibly different lifted formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_{\mathrm{usr}}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p\) and \(P_{\mathrm{sol}}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) be user and solver formulations sharing original variables \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) index the designated integral original coordinates. The translation preserves integer-feasible semantics exactly when \[\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,u)\in P_{\mathrm{usr}}:x_J\in\mathbb Z^J\}=\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,v)\in P_{\mathrm{sol}}:x_J\in\mathbb Z^J\}.\] This equality does not imply equality of the projections obtained after relaxing \(x_J\) to be continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver translation is semantically exact when the user and solver formulations project to the same original-variable points under the designated integrality restrictions; their continuous relaxations may still differ.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact interface semantics and implementation-dependent reformulation behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver may preserve an SOS or indicator interface natively, replace it by an extended linear formulation, or derive bound-dependent big-\(M\) inequalities. Semantic correctness requires equality of the represented feasible sets after designated integrality restrictions: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P_{\mathrm{sol}}\cap I)=\operatorname{proj}_x(P_{\mathrm{usr}}\cap I)\). It does not require \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P_{\mathrm{sol}})=\operatorname{proj}_x(P_{\mathrm{usr}})\) after integrality is relaxed. Consequently, equivalent solver translations can have different relaxation bounds, auxiliary-variable counts, branching behavior, and numerical conditioning; these properties cannot be inferred from the interface semantics alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver translation must preserve integer-feasible semantics, but its continuous relaxation strength and computational behavior may differ from an explicit formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver Translation Behavior

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard exact linearization of \(y=zx\) uses finite bounds \(L\le x\le U\) in \(Lz\le y\le Uz\), \(y\ge x-U(1-z)\), and \(y\le x-L(1-z)\). If \(L=-\infty\) or \(U=+\infty\), one or more coefficients are not finite, so this formulation is undefined. Replacing a missing endpoint by an arbitrary finite constant can exclude feasible points and is not a valid reformulation. A finite formulation therefore requires independently certified bounds, a different structural representation, or a solver interface capable of treating the unbounded disjunction directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard binary-product linearizations require finite source bounds; arbitrary substitute constants can invalidate the model.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Finite Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the intended relation \(y=zx\) with \(z\in\{0,1\}\) and \(0\le x\le1\). Modeling only the implication \(z=1\Rightarrow y=x\), together with \(0\le y\le1\), leaves \(y\) unrestricted by the implication when \(z=0\). Hence \((x,y,z)=(0,1,0)\) satisfies the stated model but violates \(y=zx\). Exact on/off modeling must also impose the inactive branch \(z=0\Rightarrow y=0\), either explicitly or through an equivalent formulation whose constraints enforce both branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active-state implication alone does not force the output to zero when inactive; the omitted branch admits spurious feasible points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the exact graph \(w_1=xy\) and \(w_2=x(1-y)\) on \([0,1]^2\), every point satisfies the coupling identity \(w_1+w_2=x\); therefore its convex hull also satisfies that identity. Separate McCormick relaxations are individually valid, but at \(x=y=\tfrac12\) they permit \(w_1=w_2=0\). This point violates \(w_1+w_2=x\) and hence lies outside the joint convex hull. Thus termwise validity does not imply joint ideality when terms share factors or obey algebraic identities; coupling equations or a joint formulation may be necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate valid envelopes can miss identities between terms; two coupled products give a relaxation point outside the joint convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncoupled Termwise Relaxations

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(\varnothing\ne X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R\). Consider the implication \(y=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\), encoded over \(x\in X\) by \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+M(1-y)\), where \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(U=\sup_{x\in X}a^{\mathsf T}x<\infty\). Its smallest nonnegative valid constant is \(M^\star=\max\{0,U-b\}\). Every \(M\ge M^\star\) preserves the integer feasible set. For \(M\ge0\), define \(R(M)=\{(x,y)\in X\times[0,1]:a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+M(1-y)\}\). If \(M>M^\star\), then at each fixed \(y\in[0,1]\) the row permits an additional allowance of \((M-M^\star)(1-y)\), and consequently \(R(M^\star)\subseteq R(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest valid Big-M value is the nonnegative excess of the guarded row's supremum over its bound. A larger valid value preserves the integer feasible set but weakly enlarges the continuous relaxation in proportion to the excess Big-M value and the fractional inactivity of the indicator.
knowledge_statements.title: Loose Big-M Values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-row leakage caused by combining a large deactivation coefficient with approximate integrality and row feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+M(1-y)\) with \(M\ge0\). Suppose an active-state candidate is accepted with \(y\ge1-\tau_y\), and the row is accepted when \(a^{\mathsf T}x-b-M(1-y)\le\tau_r\), where \(\tau_y,\tau_r\ge0\). Then every accepted candidate satisfies only \(a^{\mathsf T}x-b\le M\tau_y+\tau_r\). Thus, under this absolute-tolerance convention, active-row leakage grows linearly with \(M\) whenever \(\tau_y>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under explicit absolute integrality and row tolerances, an active big-M row can leak by the row tolerance plus M times the integrality tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(M,\tau_y,\tau_r\ge0\).
\(y\ge1-\tau_y\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}x-b-M(1-y)\le\tau_r\).

children.title: Scaling Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Coefficient-range, variable-scale, and unit-consistency problems that degrade reformulation performance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absolute Feasibility Tolerance Is Not Row-Scale Invariant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical nonequivalence of exact positive row scalings under a fixed absolute feasibility tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rows \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) and \(\alpha a^{\mathsf T}x\le\alpha b\), with \(\alpha>0\), define the same exact halfspace. If the scaled row is accepted whenever \(\alpha(a^{\mathsf T}x-b)\le\tau\) for fixed \(\tau>0\), its acceptance condition in the original units is \(a^{\mathsf T}x-b\le\tau/\alpha\). Hence the permitted original-unit violation becomes arbitrarily large as \(\alpha\downarrow0\) and arbitrarily small as \(\alpha\uparrow\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive row scaling preserves exact feasibility but changes the effective original-unit violation allowed by a fixed absolute tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(a,x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b\in\mathbb R\), \(\alpha>0\), and \(\tau>0\).
Feasibility is tested by the stated absolute residual rule.

notation.meaning: absolute feasibility tolerance applied to the scaled row

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Row Scaling Can Destroy Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-equivalence boundary where unequal row scaling creates arbitrarily ill-conditioned linear systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=I_2\) and \(D_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\) with \(t\ge1\). Since \(D_t\) is nonsingular, \(Ax=b\) and \(D_tAx=D_tb\) have the same exact solution set. Nevertheless, \(\kappa_\infty(A)=1\) and \(\kappa_\infty(D_tA)=t\). Thus algebraically equivalent row scalings can have arbitrarily different condition numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingular row scaling preserves exact solutions but can make an identity system arbitrarily ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: \(A=I_2\), \(b\in\mathbb R^2\), and \(D_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\) with \(t\ge1\).

notation.meaning: infinity-norm condition number of nonsingular matrix B

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-equivalence boundary where diagonal rescaling creates arbitrarily ill-conditioned linearized systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=I_2\), \(b\in\mathbb R^2\), and \(D_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\) with \(t\ge1\). Because \(D_t\) is nonsingular, \(Ax=b\) if and only if \(D_tAx=D_tb\), so premultiplication preserves the exact solution set. Nevertheless, \(\kappa_\infty(A)=1\) and \(\kappa_\infty(D_tA)=t\). Thus these algebraically equivalent systems have an arbitrarily large conditioning disparity as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive row scaling preserves the exact solution set, but unequal scale factors can make an identity system arbitrarily ill-conditioned.

children.title: Cancellation Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Loss of numerical significance caused by nearly offsetting reformulation terms or constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic relative sensitivity of a subtraction node with nearly offsetting operands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u,v\in\mathbb R\) with \(u-v\ne0\), define \(\kappa_{\mathrm{sub}}(u,v)=(|u|+|v|)/|u-v|\). If \(|e_u|\le\varepsilon|u|\) and \(|e_v|\le\varepsilon|v|\), then \(|e_u-e_v|/|u-v|\le\varepsilon\kappa_{\mathrm{sub}}(u,v)\), and this bound is attainable by admissible operand-error signs. Consequently, subtraction becomes arbitrarily ill-conditioned as \(|u-v|/(|u|+|v|)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtraction magnifies relative operand errors by the sum of operand magnitudes divided by the result magnitude, which diverges under near cancellation.
assumptions_latex: \(u,v\in\mathbb R\) and \(u-v\ne0\).
\(\varepsilon\ge0\), \(|e_u|\le\varepsilon|u|\), and \(|e_v|\le\varepsilon|v|\).

notation.meaning: componentwise relative condition number of subtraction

review_flags: Relative-error conditioning is undefined when the exact difference is zero; absolute-error analysis remains possible there.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of relative accuracy when auxiliary expressions subtract nearly equal large quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t,x\in\mathbb R\) with \(t\ne0\) and \(x\ne0\), and set \(u=t+x\), \(v=t\), and \(w=u-v=x\). Suppose \(\widehat u=u(1+\delta_u)\), \(\widehat v=v(1+\delta_v)\), and \(\widehat w=(\widehat u-\widehat v)(1+\delta_s)\), where \(|\delta_u|,|\delta_v|,|\delta_s|\le\varepsilon\). Then \(|\widehat w-x|\le\varepsilon(|u|+|v|+|x|)+\varepsilon^2(|u|+|v|)\). Consequently, as \(|x|/|t|\to0\), the relative-error bound can grow on the order of \(\varepsilon|t|/|x|\), although the exact expression remains \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting nearly equal large auxiliary values can magnify operand-rounding errors relative to the small result, even when the symbolic reformulation is exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Cancellation Pathologies

children.title: Numerical Diagnostic Signals
children.top_down_role: Solver symptoms and formulation-level indicators associated with scaling or cancellation failures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-defined residual, cancellation, and coefficient-spread signals for a linearized formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a row \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), define \(r_i=\max\{0,a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i\}/(|b_i|+\sum_j|a_{ij}x_j|)\) when the denominator is positive and \(r_i=0\) otherwise. For a subtraction \(w_k=u_k-v_k\), define \(c_k=|w_k|/(|u_k|+|v_k|)\), with \(c_k=1\) when both operands vanish. For the set \(C\) of nonzero linearization coefficients, define \(\rho=\max_{c\in C}|c|/\min_{c\in C}|c|\), with \(\rho=1\) when \(|C|\le1\). Each quantity is unchanged by positive common scaling of its associated row, subtraction operands, or coefficient set. Empty row and subtraction families contribute no signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized row violation, cancellation ratio, and coefficient dynamism provide scale-invariant formulation diagnostics with explicit zero and empty-family conventions.
assumptions_latex: All evaluated quantities are finite real numbers.
Row, subtraction-node, and nonzero-coefficient families are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_i\), \(c_k\), and \(\rho\) are well-defined and invariant under the stated positive common scalings.

cancellation ratio at subtraction node k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating numerical-risk indicators from exact feasibility, infeasibility, and optimality conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given user-selected thresholds \(\tau_f>0\), \(0<\tau_c<1\), and \(\tau_s\ge1\), the conditions \(\max_i r_i>\tau_f\), \(\min_k c_k<\tau_c\), or \(\rho>\tau_s\) may be used to flag residual, cancellation, or scaling risk, respectively, with an absent family treated as producing no flag. Threshold passage or nonpassage alone certifies neither exact feasibility, infeasibility, nor optimality; such conclusions require the solver's error model and independently valid certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thresholded residual, cancellation, and coefficient-range signals can flag numerical risk, but they are conventional alarms rather than mathematical feasibility or optimality certificates.
assumptions_latex: The signals are defined as in Scale-Invariant Numerical Diagnostic Signals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{flag}=1\) is a diagnostic condition and does not imply or refute exact feasibility, infeasibility, or optimality.
review_flags: No universal numerical values for the thresholds are asserted.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagnostic Signals Are Not Certificates
Numerical Diagnostic Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable flag combining normalized infeasibility, cancellation, and coefficient-scale diagnostics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For linearized rows \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), define normalized violation \(r_i=\max\{0,a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i\}/(1+|b_i|+\sum_j|a_{ij}x_j|)\). For each subtraction node \(w_k=u_k-v_k\), define its cancellation ratio \(c_k=|w_k|/(|u_k|+|v_k|)\), taking \(c_k=1\) when the denominator is zero. Let \(\rho\) be the ratio of the largest to smallest nonzero absolute linearization coefficient. Given positive thresholds \(\tau_f,\tau_c,\tau_s\), the formulation is numerically flagged exactly when \(\max_i r_i>\tau_f\), \(\min_k c_k<\tau_c\), or \(\rho>\tau_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation is flagged when normalized infeasibility is excessive, a subtraction is strongly cancellation-prone, or its nonzero coefficients span too large a range.
assumptions_latex: The relevant linearized rows, subtraction nodes, and nonzero coefficients are available for evaluation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(X\ne\varnothing\), and let \(f_i,\ell_i:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)\) and \(L(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\ell_i(x)\), and suppose \(\ell_i(x)\le f_i(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and every \(i\). If \(\Delta_i=\sup_{x\in X}(f_i(x)-\ell_i(x))<\infty\), then \(0\le f(x)-L(x)\le\sum_{i=1}^m\Delta_i\) for every \(x\in X\). Whenever \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(\inf_{x\in X}L(x)\) are finite, \(0\le\inf_{x\in X}f(x)-\inf_{x\in X}L(x)\le\sum_{i=1}^m\Delta_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many real-valued factors on a common nonempty domain, the pointwise and optimal-value gaps produced by summing valid underestimators are bounded by the sum of their individual worst-case errors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case optimality of the sum-of-errors bound when only factorwise error bounds are known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(m\in\mathbb N\) and \(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_m\ge0\), there exist a nonempty domain \(X\) and functions \(\ell_i\le f_i\) on \(X\) such that \(\sup_{x\in X}(f_i(x)-\ell_i(x))=\Delta_i\) for every \(i\) and \(\sup_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m(f_i(x)-\ell_i(x))=\sum_{i=1}^m\Delta_i\). Therefore no uniformly smaller bound follows from the factorwise worst-case errors alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of factorwise worst-case errors is sharp; improving it requires information that prevents the individual errors from being simultaneously large.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positional coefficient disparity and the boundary on inferring solver-search imbalance from it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge2\), \(z\in\{0,1\}^p\), \(k=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}2^jz_j\), and \(c\ne0\). Flipping \(z_j\) while fixing the other bits changes \(ck+d\) by magnitude \(|c|2^j\), so the largest-to-smallest single-bit effect ratio is \(2^{p-1}\). A scoring rule proportional to these effects inherits this ratio. The encoding alone, however, determines neither branching priorities nor search-tree size: equal, proportional, or inverse-effect scores produce different priorities from the same coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positional binary encoding creates exponentially unequal affine bit effects. It creates equally unequal branching scores only for a score rule tied to those effects and implies no solver-independent search-tree bound.
assumptions_latex: \(c\ne0\); any search-score conclusion additionally assumes a specified score rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_j|c|2^j/\min_j|c|2^j=2^{p-1}\), but the coefficients alone do not determine branching priorities or tree size.
review_flags: Search consequences are conditional on the explicitly chosen scoring rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Encoding-Induced Search Imbalance
Encoding-Induced Search Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential branching-score disparity created by positional binary coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Encode \(k\in\{0,\ldots,2^p-1\}\) as \(k=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}2^jz_j\), with \(z_j\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p\ge2\). In any affine expression \(ck+d\) with \(c\ne0\), flipping bit \(z_j\) while holding the other bits fixed changes the expression by magnitude \(|c|2^j\). Therefore the ratio between the largest and smallest single-bit effects is \(2^{p-1}\). A branching priority proportional to this coefficient effect consequently assigns exponentially disparate scores to bits solely because of the positional encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positional binary encoding gives high-order bits exponentially larger affine effects than low-order bits, so magnitude-based branching scores can become exponentially imbalanced.
assumptions_latex: \(c\ne0\), and the branching score is proportional to the absolute single-bit affine effect.

notation.meaning: Number of bits in the positional encoding.
Coefficient of the encoded integer in an affine expression.

review_flags: The algebraic disparity is explicit, but the branching-score interpretation requires a source on solver search heuristics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positional-coefficient ratio is algebraically correct, and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. However, the claimed search imbalance is conditional on a particular magnitude-proportional branching score, for which no solver or branching-heuristic source is supplied. The domain of d is also unstated. A source is required before fixing the precise solver-facing interpretation.
